We asked too much of the American university

Our one remaining functional institution is going downhill.

Noah Smith
Jul 24
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

The story of the rise and possible impending fall of the American university system is, in many ways, the story of modern America. It ties together the changes in our culture, our economy, and our politics since the mid-20th century. Understanding why universities came to be our most important and most functional institution, and why that model is now under threat, can help us understand how our country might look different going forward.

Let me try to tell a condensed version of that story.

The United States used to have a bunch of institutions that bound us together and forged us into a unified society. Many American communities were centered around churches; these facilitated networking, helped people find spouses, provided community services like day care and mutual aid, and homogenized values and culture at the local level. During the World Wars (and to a lesser extent, the Vietnam War), the military was very large and threw together Americans from various social classes. In the early postwar decades, corporations were also a unifying institution. Mass media provided us with shared cultural context. Even public transit put people of various backgrounds in close social contact on a daily basis.

In the half-century from around 1970 to 2020, those unifying institutions became much weaker. Church attendance slowly declined and then fell off a cliff in the 2010s. The military shrank into a small, professionalized volunteer force. Corporations ended their brief flirtation with lifetime employment, and outsourced many of their roles. Mass media fragmented in the age of the internet. Public transit dwindled in importance as Americans moved to the suburbs and drove.

As the country’s unifying institutions withered, one new institution attempted to step into the void: the American university. Universities were not new in the late 20th century, of course, but mass attendance certainly was. From 1970 to 2020, the share of Americans age 25-29 with a bachelor’s degree went from 16.4% to 39.6%. Around two out of three have completed some college.

College went from something that only the upper crust did, to something that most people were expected to do if they wanted to be economically successful in life. This expansion inadvertently but inevitably thrust a new role on American universities — that of a broad socially unifying institution. College was where people from a variety of backgrounds mingled and mixed — not just in classes, but in dorms, campus activities, and college towns.

College became the new church, the new military, and the neighborhood bowling alley all rolled into one. Instead of preachers homogenizing Americans’ values from the pulpit, university administrators taught college kids to value things like diversity, consent, and so on, and college students hashed out their own differences in millions of late-night dorm room discussions. Instead of meeting their first love in high school, Americans increasingly delayed sex until college; many of these relationships turned into marriages. Young people went into college as children and came out adults.

This was a heavy burden to bear for an institution that hadn’t been designed for it. But American universities were accustomed to taking on big new duties. Our universities began as essentially a copy of the British model — teaching-focused institutions designed to provide broad education and mentorship to the upper class. In the early 20th century they tacked on the German model — a research-focused lab apprenticeship system by which top scientists taught other top scientists and readied them for research jobs while also producing cutting-edge basic research.

This dual system enabled a remarkable form of cross-subsidization. Undergrad tuition payments — and state support for undergrad education, and undergrad alumni gifts — created a flood of money that paid for grad student stipends, lab facilities, professor salaries, and more. The federal government and companies also funded university research, of course, through grants and sponsorships. But undergrad money was a huge tailwind. And the prestige generated by successful and famous researchers helped universities charge undergrads more.

The hybrid of the old British and German models was naturally symbiotic, and it meant that even as America’s other institutions came under pressure, universities thrived and grew — especially once they used their prestige to attract high-paying and highly skilled foreign students from around the globe. Universities became the lynchpin of America’s research effort:

American universities had a lock on both the nation’s research output and on its production of human capital, and those roles were mutually reinforcing.

I suspect that their success at handling education and research at the same time probably gave American universities a lot of confidence about their ability to handle society and culture as well. Colleges spent more and more on dorms and “student services” and hired administrators (many of whom dealt with undergrad life) at an astonishing rate.¹

But replacing churches, the military, and the neighborhood bowling alley proved harder than replacing the corporate lab had been. There was just one basic problem with college as America’s primary unifying institution, which is that not everyone can go to college.

First of all, college is difficult. To complete college courses, you need some degree of raw intelligence, but you also need work ethic and a certain degree of independence. As much as we might like to believe otherwise, not everyone in America has those traits, and we don’t yet know how to instill them in everyone. As a result, there’s a limit to how much you can expand college enrollment — and college completion — without loosening standards.

In fact, loosening standards is exactly what American colleges have done. Universities have necessarily become less and less selective over the years, as they have taken in a larger and larger fraction of the young American population. For a while, this led to lower college completion rates, but in the 1990s, more and more students began finishing their bachelors’ degrees. Why? Because colleges implemented grade inflation, making it easier to finish school without learning the material well. Here’s Denning et al. (2021):

We find that most of the increase in graduation rates can be explained by grade inflation, and that other factors such as changing student characteristics and institutional resources play little or no role. This is because GPA strongly predicts graduation and that GPAs have been rising since the 1990s. This finding holds in national survey data and in records from 9 large public universities. We also find that at a public liberal arts college, grades increased holding performance on identical exams fixed.

At some point, though, this process hits a wall. A large fraction of young Americans just isn’t prepared for college, even with grade inflation, and doesn’t end up going. College enrollment by recent high school graduates plateaued in the early 2000s and actually fell back to early 1990s levels during and after the pandemic:

Part of this might be due to a second factor: the financial cost of college. All of those dorms and administrators cost a lot of money. Rich alumni, high-paying foreign students, and the government shouldered some of that cost, but some portion fell on students themselves. Despite increasing financial aid, net tuition (which subtracts grants and scholarships, but not student loans, from the headline figure) approximately doubled from 1990 to 2020:

Universities generally did a good job keeping prices from rising for low-income students, but for everyone else, the cost became an increasing burden.

That increasing cost burden made college no longer worth it for many people. Colleges are still creating value; don’t listen to the people who tell you that education is just “signaling”. Despite falling selectivity and rising grade inflation, the college wage premium is still at or near it’s all-time high:

But when you combine a constant benefit with rising costs, that means college is becoming a less attractive economic proposition. (Opportunity costs have been rising too, as wages increase for people who didn’t go to college.) A bunch of people are paying the steep costs of college but not seeing any economic benefit:

To exactly no one’s surprise, the NY Fed found that the students most likely not to see a financial return on their college educations were humanities and soft social science majors.

So it made sense that parents become more reluctant to pay for their kids’ college education. Student loans often stepped in to fill the breach, but after it became common knowledge that many borrowers were never able to pay off those loans, appetite for student debt began to wither as well:

Increasing public awareness of college’s worsening economic bargain made colleges even more desperate to let in anyone who was willing to pay. In the early 2020s, after the pandemic knocked some people out of school and the supply of high-paying foreign students started to dry up, many universities resorted to desperate measures, canceling standardized tests as a criterion for admission. But this led to a flood of underprepared students from bad high schools (who themselves inflated grades to an almost unbelievable degree), resulting in a ton of college students who couldn’t do basic high school math at all, and were thus unable to complete STEM degrees without essentially having them handed out.

This was basically the end of the line for the “let everyone go to college” movement. Over 280 STEM faculty at the University of California — one of the institutions that had lowered standards most aggressively — signed an open letter calling for the reimplementation of standardized testing. Even the New York Times’ editorial board agreed.

In other words, we’ve really reached the end of the rainbow in terms of increasing college attainment. What this means is that college acts as a unifying institution for only a fraction of the American populace — somewhere between the 40% of Americans who complete their bachelor’s and the 60% who complete any college at all.

Having college be our substitute for church, military, and bowling alley has left us a deeply divided nation, both politically and culturally. Education, rather than income or even race², has become the key dividing line of American politics. The longer you spend within the walls of our one remaining unifying institution, the more progressive you become:

Universities are now factories that create the Democratic voter base — not because professors indoctrinate their students with Marxism or Critical Race Theory, but because universities bring together people who are already progressive and isolate them from conservatives. Free from daily interaction with dissenting ideas, progressives drift farther and farther from the broader American culture outside their bubble.

This has become progressivism’s Achilles heel. Extreme sorting has caused them to believe that ideas the rest of the world considers radical are not only normal but inevitable. The progressive bubble lives on after college — in the human networks forged at universities, in professional jobs where everyone went to similar colleges, in coastal metropolises filled with college graduates, in media and social media aimed at educated audiences, and so on. It’s no surprise that so many educated progressives were utterly blindsided by the rise of Trump, and by his reelection in 2024.

College had become “church for progressives”, but it could only be that for 40% of the country.

Universities’ progressive monoculture has also begun to weaken their scholarship, and their reputation. I remember one day in 2011, when I asked an English PhD student at the University of Michigan what the social benefit of his research was. Momentarily at a loss for an answer, he eventually told me that research into English literature could help marginalized people.

What I glimpsed that day was the rise of scholar-activism. With increasingly few conservatives or even moderates remaining among the professoriate, the notion that research should seek objective truth becomes ever more distant and abstract. By 2023, social science scholars were writing editorials defending the production of fabricated research, as long as those fabrications served a righteous activist cause. This lowers the quality of research, of course. But it can also reduce society’s trust in the professoriate, and a recent report commissioned by Vanderbilt and Washington University makes the case that a tipping point has been reached:

In recent years [some people have complained] that the traditional goal of coming to understand the human world through careful scholarship has been subordinated to, or even displaced by, a “political” goal: the aim of realizing a conception of social justice nowadays associated with the progressive left. More specifically, the complaint is that scholarly standards for the assessment of academic work have been distorted within these disciplines both to privilege work on topics that are taken to be relevant to social justice, and much more importantly, to replace more traditional standards for assessing academic scholarship with political standards designed to ensure that only politically acceptable work is published, taught and valorized…

As we will emphasize [in this report], there is serious scholarship in every field we have studied, and at their best, the humanities and the social sciences are as rigorous and as fruitful as they have ever been. Taken as a whole, however, our review of the disciplines paints a mixed picture. Every field we have studied shows some signs of the pathologies sketched above: a deterioration in scholarly standards fueled by the substitution of political criteria for properly scholarly criteria in the assessment of research and a more general repudiation of long-standing ideals of rigor and objectivity. In some fields (e.g., philosophy) the problems are largely confined to a single subfield focused on a charged topic. In others (e.g., history), while there are streams of scholarship in which standards have been politicized in problematic ways, they run alongside more dominant streams in which a wide range of views is tolerated, and appropriately scholarly standards are brought to bear. In the most extreme cases (e.g., anthropology), we see a widespread deterioration in scholarly standards grounded in a pervasive repudiation of ideals of objectivity together with a toxic intellectual climate in which reasonable dissent on politically charged topics is routinely suppressed and punished.

Scholar-activism hasn’t entirely taken over academia, of course — not even close. But it’s rise has predictably brought on a ferocious backlash from the political right. Donald Trump’s attacks on science are a direct response to the progressive ideology espoused by many modern researchers and reflected in academic hiring and granting. They are a foolish and destructive response, to be sure — kind of like slicing off a finger to get rid of a wart. But something like this was inevitable.

And it’s worth noting that not all of Trump’s science policies are destructive. In a recent memo, Trump promised to redirect federal grant funding away from universities and toward individual scientists — basically, removing university’s role as a middleman in terms of directing funds. Of course weakening universities as an institution is part of Trump’s motivation for doing this, removing a layer of bureaucracy in the research process is probably a good idea on the merits; in fact, it’s based on a proposal by the Institute for Progress, which is definitely not a conservative institution or invested in the culture wars.

But in any case, the American university system now finds itself buffeted by multiple crises — the plateau of students’ willingness and ability to pay, and the conservative backlash over progressive scholar-activism. Polls show that both Democrats and Republicans are becoming steadily less confident in what was once America’s most functional institution:

But their reasons for being dissatisfied are probably different. Some are enraged at high costs and uncertain economic benefits, while others, probably mostly Republican, are incensed over ideology on campus:

Ultimately, both of these problems are downstream of universities’ expanding role. When universities became the unifying social institution that ties nearly half of America together, it required explosive spending on administration and student life that drove up costs, made college a worse financial proposition, and ultimately enraged many of the very people it was meant to benefit. But it also created a bubble-like progressive monoculture, gatekept by intelligence and conscientiousness and money, that generated a conservative backlash as soon as the monoculture began to promote its ideas outside the bubble.

This is not the only challenge facing universities, of course. Other factors, like the impending “enrollment cliff” due to America’s shrinking population of teenagers, or AI changing the kind of curriculum that delivers good economic returns, are beyond universities’ control. But had universities not expanded their remit from research and the transfer of knowledge to cultural unification, they would be far better prepared to deal with exogenous headwinds.

This doesn’t mean the American university is finished. As long as in-person human-to-human teaching and collaboration continue to be important, the synergistic fusion of teaching and research that the United States discovered in the 20th century will continue to be valuable.

But in order to survive and thrive, I think that universities need to rethink their more recently assumed role as an engine of social integration. The university can’t be the Universe; students should be encouraged to have lives outside campus, and seek both ideas and friends outside the small circles of their classes and dorms and clubs. And students should understand that campus administration is not an all-powerful fairy godmother who can make anything unpleasant go away and give young people a guarantee of romance, adventure, and meaning. Bloated administrations and student life spending, rather than research, should bear the brunt of whatever funding cuts are forced on the university system.

More broadly, America needs something besides universities to bind us together into a single people, because by their very nature, universities will always be for only a fraction of the populace. As for what those other institutions can be, I don’t yet have a complete answer, and it deserves more time and thought than this paragraph will allow.

Share

1

I went to college a quarter century ago, which was fairly early in this process. But already, I felt like college, as an institution, had made an implicit promise to me to fill the holes that America’s other institutions had been unable to fill. I came in expecting to live among a society of my peers, instead of being one of the “gifted” kids. I expected to have adventures of the kind that growing up in a small Texas city simply didn’t offer. I knew lots of other kids who felt the same way. Stanford University, with its full-service “residential education” experience, seemed to promise to give me all that adventure, personal growth, community, and self-discovery as a sort of guided tour. Of course it didn’t work out quite like I anticipated, but all in all I think it was a good experience.

2

With, of course, the notable exception of Black voters.

Elon Musk, the New Hero of Populism

The useful narcissism of the new class of oligarchs

Paul Krugman
Jul 23
 
READ IN APP
 

Republicans have settled on their midterm argument: Democrats are all Communists. As an election strategy, this is as lame as it is ludicrous. But there is a small kernel of political reality underlying the new right-wing red-baiting: The emergence of a widespread public backlash against the extreme concentration of wealth in the hands of billionaires.

This backlash shows up in multiple surveys. According to the Harris Billionaires Survey, 73 percent of Americans believe that wealth inequality is a serious national issue, up from 66 percent in 2022. A UMass Amherst poll found 58 percent of Americans saying that billionaires are a threat to democracy, with 45 percent saying that America is an oligarchy, “a government in which a small group exercises control especially for corrupt and selfish purposes.” Only 28 percent disagreed.

And as I noted last week, citing research from political scientist Andrew Hall, Democratic fundraising has recently begun to lean heavily into denunciations of the undue influence of billionaires:

So if you define anyone who raises concerns about the wealth and political power of billionaires as a Communist, well, in that sense you are defining a majority of Americans as communists.

Why is the public backlash against billionaires going viral now? This is an interesting question, since both the concentration of wealth at the top and political spending by billionaires have been increasing for decades. For example, the Koch Brothers have been donating to the Federalist Society, the clique of right-wing legal lobbyists who created the Roberts Supreme Court, since the early 1980s. Fossil fuel interests have been spreading climate disinformation since global warming began showing up in the data. Political spending by billionaires has been immense for more than a decade, although it reached new heights to help Trump win the presidency and to win Republican congressional seats in the 2024 election. Why, then, has it taken so long for the popular billionaire backlash to reach critical mass?

One answer is that Trump has brought American oligarchy out of the shadows and into the spotlight. As I noted last week, the spectacle of “the cavalcade of fawning tech bros at the Trump inauguration” was a clear wake-up call. Yet the display of billionaire fealty to Trump, I would argue, is part of a larger dynamic in which the new generation of American oligarchs have chosen to make themselves public figures and hence public targets.

The fact is that billionaires have had immense political power for decades, but they chose to exercise that power from the shadows, veiling their actions through patriotic sounding right-wing PACs and think tanks. Only political junkies understood what was going on underneath the surface.

Today, however, the new generation of the hyper-wealthy are out there and in your face, flaunting their influence rather than concealing it. And the poster child for this change is, of course, Elon Musk.

To understand the significance of this change in the behavior of the hyper-wealthy, it’s useful to compare the lists of top individual donors compiled by OpenSecrets in different recent elections, specifically 2016 and 2024.

In 2016, the top 100 donors split their spending almost equally between Republicans and Democrats, with 9 of the top 20 strongly pro-Democratic. This was unusual and surely reflected the fact that a significant number of Republican donors were appalled by Donald Trump. But by 2024, when Trump was again the GOP standard-bearer, most of these qualms and scruples had disappeared: the top 100 donors spent more than 3 times as much on Republicans as they did on Democrats, and only 5 of the top 20 supported Democrats. This, after Trump’s authoritarianism and corruption had become plainly evident.

More to the point, consider who the top Republican donors were in 2016. People who follow politics closely have long been aware of the key roles in right-wing politics played by Sheldon and Miriam Adelson (gambling money), Paul Singer (vulture capitalist), Robert Mercer (computer scientist turned hedge funder), and Richard Uilein (shipping). But none of them sought the celebrity limelight, and it was always an uphill struggle to raise public awareness of their malign policy and political influence.

The 2024 list still includes many of the traditionally quiet oligarchs. But, unlike before, it also includes a number of right-wing billionaires who love to put themselves in the public eye and offer their views on everything from fiscal policy to culture. These include Ken Griffin (hedge fund), Marc Andreesen (tech/venture capital), and Stephen Schwarzman (private equity.)

And topping the list is, of course, Musk. He spent much of last year de facto running large parts of the U.S. government, slashing spending in ways that failed to save taxpayer money but did lead to serious degradation of government functioning and have already led to hundreds of thousands of deaths. Moreover, Musk’s narcissism – much like Donald Trump – has compelled him to make himself the center of attention in press conferences held in the Oval Office. And, like Trump, he doesn’t learn from his mistakes. He is now noisily weighting in not just on politics, the evils of wokeness and nonwhite immigration, and so on, but on The Odyssey. (He hated it and predicted, wrongly, that it would be a box-office disaster.)

The larger point here is that there has been an important transition in America from the days when oligarchic power was mostly exercised in the shadows to the current era of flamboyant and extremist displays of billionaire influence.

What caused the change? At least part of the cause is a shift in the origins of great wealth, from fossil fuels (e.g. the Koch brothers) and other traditional industries to the tech broligarchy. As Henry Farrell argues, many tech billionaires are caught up in the cult of “founders,” believing themselves to be superior beings entitled to special privilege and universal acclaim — which means putting themselves out in public. I would add that the tech industry has suffered a precipitous decline in public perceptions since its peak around 2015 — and the fawning tech bros at the Trump inauguration were, to a large extent, former culture heroes who want their glory days back.

So surely part of the reason a majority of Americans now say that democracy is being undermined, that billionaires are running everything, is that the billionaires themselves are out there boasting about their influence.

And their brazenness is actually doing the rest of us a favor. Mobilizing against the oligarchic threat to democracy was hard when the oligarchs were operating from the shadows. It’s easier now that some of them are out in the open.

Elon Musk makes an unlikely hero of populism. But his odious and unbridled narcissism may very well help save the American republic.

Landlords are inevitable

State control doesn’t make tradeoffs go away.

Matthew Yglesias
Jul 23
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

I’ve had three different landlords as an adult. One of them did a pretty good job but was obstinate about trying to charge more rent than the place was worth. Another was a total catastrophe in almost every respect. The third was basically fine, except he decided he wanted to get out of the landlording business and sell the house I was renting, so I had to leave.

I don’t know if my experience is typical, but I do think it’s indicative of the kinds of problems people have with landlords. They can be shitty. They can be good but charge a premium for not being shitty. Or they can be good and charge reasonable rent and then realize that it’s not necessarily worth the trouble.

This is one reason I think the idea of large institutional landlords is underrated.

A big player can try to do what Walmart or Chipotle or Hilton Hotels does and actually build a reputation for providing reasonable service at reasonable prices and benefit from scale. Mom and pop can’t.

Regardless, though, I understand why people often find landlords frustrating. And I get the appeal of this line in the new Democratic Socialists of America platform about how under socialism “you don’t pay a mortgage or have a landlord, because comfortable housing is a human right.”

But this doesn’t make sense. If you live in a home you don’t own, then you have a landlord. It’s just that the landlord will be a public sector entity rather than a private one.

It’s worth thinking about, say, public school: Kids have a right to a free public education in the United States, but that doesn’t mean schools don’t have rules.

It does mean, in practice, that it’s harder to get kicked out of public school than private school. But from many families’ perspectives, that’s actually a downside of public school. One child’s right to his place in public school is another child’s need to put up with disorderly behavior.

In other regards, the dynamic flips — a public school can be tougher with grades because it has less need to please the customers.

The point, though, is that while a public school can be managed in many ways, the mere fact that it’s public doesn’t answer the question of how it should be managed or guarantee that it’ll be managed well. And the exact same thing is true of a public housing project. You might not call the person in charge of it “the landlord,” but someone is making decisions about who can live where and under what terms and what happens if the elevator breaks.

Real scarcities matter

The D.S.A. view is that housing, along with food, energy, medicine, and transportation, is one of several consumption goods that are so necessary for life as to be too important to leave up to the whims of the market.

Note, though, that this is more or less already how we think about food.

We have more than our share of problems in this country, but thanks to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and America’s food banks, we don’t have people starving to death. State action to support the poor is one important reason for that. But part of why SNAP works as well as it does is that groceries are objectively abundant in America. Of course, on any given day, people looking to feed their families may feel the squeeze. But that’s because Americans looking to feed their families are generally aiming for something more than basic caloric sustenance. If you’re willing to shop frugally, food is pretty cheap. As a result, a public sector program to give people money to buy food can successfully feed them without breaking the bank.

We have a comparable program, Section 8 vouchers, for housing.

The narrow problem with Section 8 is that unlike SNAP, it’s not funded in a way that ensures all eligible families get a voucher. About three-quarters of the people who theoretically qualify do not receive housing assistance.

The deeper problem, though, is that there aren’t enough homes for everyone. If I give you some money, point you at a supermarket, and tell you to go buy a cheap meal, you’ll easily walk out with a cheap meal. Housing is not like that at all.

Medical care and energy are in less acutely short supply, but they still suffer from real scarcities. There aren’t a lot of unemployed doctors wandering the streets of America. The provision (or not) of health insurance and the financing of health care services are important topics. But if some people are forgoing large amounts of useful health care, that’s at least in part a supply-side issue.

And the United Kingdom has shown us over the past five or 10 years that if you starve a totally public system of resources, you can still have acute supply shortages.

Here in the United States, mass transit systems are all publicly owned. But that doesn’t guarantee that service will be frequent or convenient. To make that happen, cities need to actually build trains or buy buses and hire drivers and otherwise do the work of managing complicated systems. The appeal of the SNAP model is precisely that it lets you skip all that. Walmart figures out how to run a store and the government focuses on making sure poor people have income support.

In terms of energy, the United States has all kinds of utility models. There are tons of publicly owned electrical utilities in this country. Most of them are very small, but there’s also the Tennessee Valley Authority. Lots of people are customers of private regulated utilities. Some are vertically integrated (i.e., the utility owns the power plants), while others are restructured (i.e., the utility buys power on a market).

There are pros and cons to all of these models, but none of them have made electricity free or eliminated pollution or done any of the other good things you might want to accomplish. That’s because making clean energy abundant requires all this object-level work — you need to build the solar farms and the batteries and the transmission lines and the nuclear reactors.

You can’t just say, “well, it’s a common good now, problem solved” when you haven’t actually solved anything.

Location, location, location

This is particularly true for housing, where even though it’s a commodity that’s bought and sold for profit, the status quo is that there’s no free market in building.

You could completely eliminate the capitalistic aspects of this system and all the problems would recur.

Say you’ve been living somewhere for 10 years and now suddenly, for whatever reason, way more people are interested in living in that location. Is the fair system to re-run a new lottery for this suddenly in-demand location, in which case you and other incumbent residents might be displaced? Or is it fairer to say whoever was there first gets the prime location forever? What if it’s a three-bedroom unit and your kids are all grown up and there are young couples with babies who need larger dwellings? If we stick with continuity, we’re going to have a situation where none of the kids who grew up in this neighborhood are able to live there as adults — where will they go? Do we turn farms into new housing developments or are those beloved aspects of the landscape?

It seems to me that if a given location is in high demand — in the socialist utopia, this would be oversubscribed lotteries rather than high prices — the most reasonable step is to build more there.

But who decides this? Is it at the discretion of the housing authority or is it decided mechanically as a result of the lottery? Does the local community get a say in disruptive changes? Aren’t politicians going to be inclined to listen to the local community and not build, whatever the formal process is?

Having won the lottery to secure a good house wouldn’t have financial value in this system — you couldn’t sell the right to live there. Of course, people would try, and there would have to be Sublet Cops trying to stop them. But the good house would still be valuable, and NIMBYs would still try to protect that value. And none of the fundamentals of land use and planning will have changed because we’re already talking about a centrally planned system. And just as a public school needs to decide on rules of discipline, so would a public landlord — what would the terms of occupancy be? What would happen if you violated them?

I don’t deny that abolishing all private homeownership in the United States would be a big deal, because obviously it would be a huge deal. But it would be a big deal that paradoxically wouldn’t change any of the main pain points.

The ultimate “tenant’s right” is exit

One big upside of a free market is that if you’re not happy with the person on the other side of the transaction, you can just leave. I went to a restaurant the other day, looked at the menu, and ordered something that struck me as a little overpriced but that I was hoping would be good. But when the food came, it wasn’t very good. So I’m not going to do that again.

When a landlord screws you over, it’s harder to just pick up and move because the logistics are disruptive and the change can’t be made instantly.

Still, the fundamentals of a healthy housing market should be that if people aren’t happy with the quality of service provided by their landlord, they can leave. All the strong tenant protection laws in the world can’t come close to matching the power of the ability to exit a bad situation.

Indeed, tenant protections can be a double-edged sword. In D.C., at one point they made it so landlords couldn’t evict violent tenants, which is a “pro-tenant” policy only if you take a very dim view of the behavior of the average renter. The right that people need is the right to move, ideally without moving across the country or necessarily even across the city. That requires an abundant supply of housing in the locations where people want to live.

The risk of government-run housing is eliminating all possibility of exit. There’s just one landlord, and if they’re doing a bad job, you’re stuck. You haven’t eliminated landlords — you’ve created a universal landlording monopoly.

Subscribed

Don’t get me wrong — the status quo housing situation facing young people is genuinely dire. But we need solutions that work. Less-constrained zoning, more access to credit, and even really boring stuff like making the unemployment insurance system work better for construction workers will make things better by giving people more exit options. Trying to ban landlords won’t, because at the end of the day the landlord is inevitable and unavoidable. Competition is the only remedy.

Will A.I. take your job? Mine? Everyone’s?

Timothy Lee from Understanding AI tells me I’m wrong about this.

Matthew Yglesias
Jul 23
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

Concern about artificial intelligence and the labor market is an interesting kind of horseshoe. On the one hand, all indications are that normal people have a lot of anxiety about the way this technology might impact their jobs and employment prospects. On the other hand, the leading figures in the A.I. industry all believe their work is going to lead to massive short-term labor-market disruption and, in the longer term, the total displacement of human workers.

But between those peaks of anxiety is a middle ground of economists and journalists saying this is overhyped.

Economists know that Luddites have worried about automation leading to permanent disemployment for hundreds of years, underrating the benefits of productivity improvements. And cynical journalists think A.I. companies are just talking their own books when they speak of sweeping technological transformation.

I mentioned offhand on an earlier episode that I am largely on the combined side of the savvy industry insiders and the ignorant masses — I think economists are peddling a misguided midwit take that overindexes on 250 years of Industrial Revolution relative to the full sweep of history. Timothy Lee of the great A.I.-focused Substack Understanding AI heard me offer this opinion and suggested coming on the show to debate it.

My Co-Host Jerusalem Demsas is largely on Tim’s side. They think A.I. will change labor markets but in a broadly normal way — that it will displace jobs but do so at a gradual pace that is similar to how work and the economy normally transform over time. They call attention to the fact that most jobs consist of a big bundle of tasks, so as some tasks get automated, people will shift the balance of their work rather than the job evaporating altogether. They’re also both believers in the value of the “human touch” — the idea that, in many contexts, people willingly pay a premium for the benefits of human interaction.

I think this is all a little too pessimistic about the pace of technological change and too rosy about the virtues of actual human beings. The human touch can be great, but lots of people are mediocre and half of them are below average. You by definition can’t replace a Lionel Messi or a Lamine Yamal with a robot, but the vast majority of people aren’t superstars at anything, much less in a job where using automation would break the rules.

Last but not least, I make the case that I am not a “doomer.” What I am actually expressing is extreme optimism about the ability of technology to make human toil unnecessary — I just think it’s important that we take this scenario seriously so it is managed for broad human benefit.

Jerusalem, Tim, and I get into all of it on this week’s episode. Watch or listen wherever you get your podcasts.

Paid subscribers can watch the ad-free embedded video at the top of this post and read the full transcript below.

WATCH THE EPISODE ON YOUTUBE

New episodes post every Thursday.

Jerusalem Demsas: Hi everyone. My name is Jerusalem Demsas.

Matthew Yglesias: I’m Matthew Yglesias.

Jerusalem Demsas: And welcome to The Argument. Today is our first episode with a guest. Welcome, Timothy Lee of Understanding AI.

Timothy Lee: Hi there. I’m thrilled to be here.

Jerusalem Demsas: Well, Tim, you’re a big fan of the show, so you heard a stray comment made, I think it was by me several episodes ago, where I just mentioned that Matt and I had different views on AI and jobs. And you are a perfect person to come talk to us about this.

So, Matt, you’re the one who has kind of like a different perspective than me and Tim. So, why don’t you start? What do you think is going to happen?

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah. I have the view, you know — we can never decide which one is contrarian and which one isn’t — but I feel like both the founders and executives of the AI labs and normal people agree that, like, AI is going to be incredibly disruptive to labor markets and create large-scale job losses and, like, wrenching social and economic transformation. And I think that they — both the people who know what they’re talking about and the people who don’t know what they’re talking about — are correct. And I think there’s this kind of, like, midwit economics PhD view that, like, “No, no, no, people always think there’s gonna be these disruptions and, like, it’s fine.” And I don’t think that that’s right.

Like, I agree that there will be some frictions, some delays, some stumbles. Nothing ever goes quite as smoothly as, like, the guy running a startup thinks it’s going to go. But, fundamentally, on a timescale that I think is really rapid by the standards of American politics, I think that this is going to be a huge issue, especially the next time we hit an actual economic downturn and companies face real meaningful pressure to cut costs. I think there’s going to be a big issue here and that the voters are right to be concerned about this.

The AI lab leaders, I mean, I guess they’ve changed their message a little bit because they were told by their lobbyists and pollsters that this is not what voters want to hear. But I think, like, there’s a big — I don’t even want to say problem — but, like, a big issue is going to be facing us in the, it’s sooner than, you know, political people want to believe.

Jerusalem Demsas: Well, I think — can we get more specific here? Because I also think AI is going to be a huge thing that’s going to cause, like, massive disruptions and change how the economy works. But I think, specifically, the area where I think me and you are different is you think that, like — and maybe I’m wrong here — my perception of your views is that AI is going to wipe out white-collar jobs in the next decade.

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah, I mean, I think that, look, so there’s always sort of two things you have to talk about when technology and job disruption, right? There’s specific displacement, where individual roles, occupational categories, whatever, either go away or they shrink dramatically in response to technological change. And then there’s the prospect of wholesale labor displacement, right?

Like, there’s way fewer horses today than there were 150 years ago, and that’s because internal combustion engines, like, really, really, really eliminated the need for horse labor. It didn’t, you know — not down to zero. My father-in-law works with a horse. But, you know, it’s unusual.

There’s also a question of timelines and scales, right? So, over time, we see a lot of kind of micro displacement of jobs by technology. But usually it’s one category, another category. These categories are not that large. And so, society as a whole does not have, like, a crisis that’s like, “Oh my God, we don’t have neighborhood photo development shops anymore.”

Like, those did go away, and a lot of jobs related to analog photography went away. And that was a problem for the people in those jobs, but it wasn’t like a macroeconomic phenomenon.

I think, at a minimum with AI, because AI is fairly general purpose, we’re going to see those kind of analog-to-digital-photography scale displacements hitting a bunch of different sectors simultaneously, such that it’s not going to be obvious what the transition is or what happens to people. It may be that in the long, long run, it’s all fine and it all reallocates. But, the more you start thinking about the long run, the more you also have to think that robotics will advance to match up with things.

Right now, I mean, you can’t replace, like, anything that involves people using their hands with an AI. AI hands are just not that good. But counting on that as, like, the long-term salvation of human labor strikes me as, like, actually pretty dubious.

You know, and if you go back — like, when Karel Čapek was writing about robots 100 years ago, the assumption was that AI would displace manual labor first. You know, that it would be sort of easier to fold laundry than, like, make charts and write code.

Yeah, that turns out to not be the case, but, like, folding laundry is itself a coding problem. So, you know, like, I just — I think that, like, taking refuge in the limits of physical bandwidth is probably a mistake if we’re saying, “OK, you know, we’re gonna have less white-collar work, but people will shift into things that are more tangible and blue collar” — like, it’s going to come for that as well.

Jerusalem Demsas: Tim, what’s your reaction to all this?

Timothy Lee: So, I think an important thing to remember here is that when we think about a job, it’s often a mix of a bunch of different tasks. And I think you’re seeing this the most with programming, which is the profession that’s most impacted, I think, right now by progress in AI models.

We have these coding agents that can do — in some sense, can do — most of what we think about as the programmer’s job. And I know a fair number of programmers. They are telling me that their work is dramatically changing. They can give the coding agents a big chunk of their jobs. They go off and write this, fix this bug or add this feature, and they can do most of the work.

And a couple of things are happening there. One is, obviously, people just are producing more code. There’s features they would have not had time to produce in the past that they’re producing more of.

But the other thing is that it turns out that, like, the job of a programmer will — like, formally, like, the main thing they’re doing is writing code — there’s actually a lot of other stuff they do that kind of comes around the code writing.

There’s a newsletter I really like called AI as Normal Technology that recently had a post where they talked about jobs as a sandwich — white-collar jobs — where first you have to decide what you’re going to do, then you do it, and then you, like, deliver it to the customer. And so, a lot of what programmers do these days is actually, you know, talking to users, talking to their boss, doing testing of the software after it’s produced.

And, increasingly, I think what you’re gonna see is that we’ll still have programmers, and the actual writing of code is going to be a smaller and smaller part of their job. But people are still going to want people involved in, like, deciding what the coding agent needs to do and then deciding whether it did a good job, because that inherently involves elements of politics, elements of building relationships with other people. Often it means going to a place and seeing what’s happening, things like that.

I think this is likely to be true across the economy, that there are going to be some aspects of most jobs. Matt mentioned photo development. I think one reason that didn’t lead to mass displacement is that, even before the digital revolution, you had a lot of photo development shops that were integrated into Walmarts or drugstores or whatever. And so, when that process got more efficient, these retailers reallocated the time of those photo developers to providing some other service at the store.

And so, I think, for the most part, that’s what I expect to happen. I think there are very few jobs that are so purely automatable that we’ll just get rid of them.

I think there are some of those. I’m definitely not saying there’s not going to be any job loss, but I think more than people expect, you’re going to have jobs that are a mix of automatable tasks and non-automatable tasks, and the nature of jobs will shift over time. But that I think very few jobs are likely to go away entirely.

Jerusalem Demsas: I basically have two broad thoughts on this question of whether you see wide-scale white-collar jobs get eliminated. First is that we see right now that AI can do a ton of tasks — so many tasks that I do in my job. It can technically write articles — whether you think they’re as good as ones that I would write, that’s up to you to decide. But it can technically write articles, it can write emails. It could, you know, draft speeches. It could write my tweets. It could do many, many of the tasks that, like, make up my job.

It could even, like, pull together performance reviews. It can write, like, onboarding documents for people. It could help me with financial decisions to make for the — like, there’s so many things about my job that could be automated with AI.

But, like, this, there’s this question of, like, what is a job? And one concept I think is, like, super, super useful is this O-ring concept within economics, which comes from the really terrible tragedy of the Challenger, where it’s a spaceship that blows up as a result of one small failure of one piece. And Alex Imas, who’s an economist in this space, has a really good analogy to cooking, where he’s like, you could have a world-class chef do everything perfectly to make this great meal, but if someone oversalts it, the meal is inedible. It doesn’t matter that you cooked the foie gras perfectly or that you got these ingredients sourced from this perfect area. If you oversalt the dish, you fucked up the whole meal.

And I think this is, like, something really important to think about with jobs, which is, like, I think something that, like, many AI developers don’t often see is that there are tons of these jobs which get, like, degraded as email jobs or, like, middle management jobs or whatever, which have all these components within them that are — the task may be automatable, but there’s something specific that needs to be done that is important for humans to do. And then, like, secondarily, that, like, if one thing goes wrong, it fucks up the whole system. And so, I think that both of those arguments make it difficult for me to see how you actually end up automating all white-collar jobs.

Matthew Yglesias: OK. But I think we need to look at both of these kind of examples that you guys are talking about and think about them in terms of growth and shifts in firms and elasticity of demand, right?

So, when productivity in a field increases, right? So that, like, one person can accomplish more work than they used to be able to. The impact of that on employment in that field is ambiguous, right?

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Because if what you’re doing is very, very expensive, but also very, very useful to people, the fact that one person can now achieve more means that the price goes down, means that people consume more of it, right?

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: So, like, you know, the first iPhone, right? Like, cost a fortune, and not that many people bought it. And as we got better at making smartphones, there were, like, more people — were working in making smartphones, making smartphone apps. So, computer programming, for now, I think, has proven to be a field where there is, like, a lot of demand for computer programming.

So, as the AI has made it possible to automate parts of the software development stack, you’ve had, like, a labor market hiccup around that, where, like, temporarily, a lot of companies seemed like they were pausing hiring or were like, “I’m not sure what we really want to do here.” And it’s now picked back up as we’ve said, “OK, what our developers are going to do is different from what they were doing five years ago, but we still have clients, we still have software that we want to ship, and we still have jobs for humans to do.”

So, Jerusalem, you were talking about AI at The Argument does a lot of work, but it has not displaced anybody’s human labor because there’s these O-ring tasks you need to do. But also, The Argument is brand new. Like, The Argument didn’t exist three years ago. I think that The Argument is publishing more material than the number of people on your team could have put out, in part because, like, you guys use AI to do things.

Jerusalem Demsas: Like, well, to be clear, we do not use AI to write our articles.

Matthew Yglesias: No, no, no, no, no.

Yes, but I mean, like, you used AI to, like, help research things that you needed to do to, like, get the pitch together, right? Like, I use AI to produce Slow Boring‘s work — not to, like, write the articles, but, like, my charts look better because I’m using AI for it. I get literature reviews from Claude.

Jerusalem Demsas: But also it just, like, saves you tons of time on other things. Like, you don’t have to do your business, you know, tax forms in the same monotonous way.

Matthew Yglesias: Right, exactly. So, small-scale startups are becoming more efficient.

Now, in journalism, we’ve seen a lot of this over the past 25 years, right? And the upshot is that it’s not like nobody is employed in journalism compared to how it was 25 years ago, but many fewer people are employed in the field of journalism. And yet, readers have plenty of stuff to read, right? Like, the internet has made the whole journalism field dramatically more productive, and there isn’t the kind of elasticity response that we’re seeing with computer programmers.

People aren’t saying, “Oh, any individual journalist can produce so much more than they could in the ‘90s, and therefore we want to read 50x the amount of stuff.” We have Substacks, we have cool small magazines starting up, we have The New York Times — has become an iconic global brand — but journalism as a field is shrinking under pressure from technology.

Jerusalem Demsas: Isn’t this just how you define the field of journalism? There’s so many more creators, people who comment on the news. I just think that you’re — again, like all things, it’s just like a market definition problem. Like, I’m not really sure you’re right that, like, the field of journalism is shrinking if you count people who are now doing independent journalism, doing Substacks.

Like, you can say, like, that’s, like, worse quality, but, like, the number of people producing content that, like, people classify as part of their news consumption, like, seems like that has to have gone up.

Matthew Yglesias: Wait, no, I don’t... Well, I mean, look, whatever — however the BLS qualifies, you know, reporters and editors and whatever, like, that line is going down, right?

And, I mean, just to say, like, these are two different trajectories that we can see with different kinds of fields in different places. And, like, a famous one is when ATMs first rolled out, a lot of people were like, “Oh my God, there’s not gonna be any bank tellers anymore.” And then it turned out, like, there were still plenty of bank tellers, because the number of tellers per branch went down, but banks decided it would be good to have more branches than ever because it’s cheaper to operate a branch.

So, in the short term, like, the elasticity was saving bank teller as an occupational category, although bank tellers as a share of the population were going down during this period. Then, because of mobile banking apps, we actually did get a switch, and now there’s fewer bank tellers than there used to be.

So, you know, the world is a little bit more complicated than you might think. It’s hard to just sort of guess at firsthand what is and isn’t going to displace work.

But just to say that, like, what Tim was saying about, like, jobs shifting, and things recombine — like, that’s all true and it does happen, but, like, occupational categories really do shrink under technological pressure.

So, going back to computer programming, because I think the way this is going to go is that it’s not that AI is going to replace computer programmers. It’s that computer programmers, being made much more productive thanks to AI, are going to start being able to do dramatically more custom software for different kinds of people, for different kinds of companies.

That things where it used to be, you know, you could throw a lot of resources into making Google Docs, right? Something very broad, very general, very useful to people. We would use these big software platforms, but they’re not specific enough to meet these O-ring kind of problems.

But because small groups of programmers can get so much more done with AI, you’re going to start seeing — you know, whether it’s IBM, other consulting firms — really working on, like, how can we solve these problems for you, individual company, to get more done with fewer people? Because we’ve never really had that yet.

And the big AI labs themselves are so focused on “Let’s use AI to build the next foundational model,” right? Like, OpenAI and Google and Anthropic are, like, not trying to make line-of-business software right now, but their customers are going to start using it. And then the customers of those companies are going to start saying, “You know what? We need way fewer accountants than we used to, because you can dump a bunch of stuff into an AI and it can do the analysis.”

And sure, among other things, for legal purposes, you need at least one human accountant in your giant company to sign the document and say, “I am accepting legal liability for this being totally fraudulent.” But, like, you know, that’s still a lot of potential automation happening there.

And, unlike with, say, telephone operators or other — or bank tellers — we’re going to see this hitting a bunch of different occupational categories simultaneously. And people are going to say, like, “What am I supposed to do with myself?”

Timothy Lee: So, I think there’s a big question here about time scales. Because I don’t think I — at the most abstract level, I don’t disagree with any of what Matt’s saying. I do think that over the next 20, 30 years, you’re going to see pretty significant adjustments in the mix of what kind of jobs people have and both what jobs people do within jobs, but also, yeah, I think some job categories will shrink, some will grow.

But if it takes 20 or 30 years, that’s long enough that somebody who starts their career now can have most of their career before — most of the job losses can be through attrition or people kind of voluntarily switch to other jobs as opposed to mass layoffs.

So I think it really matters: Is this something going to happen over five years or 20 years? And I think that’s partly a question about AI model capabilities.

And one of the things that I think is important right now is that AI models are very good at well-defined kind of short tasks — things that take a few minutes or in some cases a few hours — but they’re really not good at longer-term tasks, and they’re particularly not good at maintaining context over long periods of time.

I mean, a lot of what I think Jerusalem, as the leader of your organization, do is you have the big picture of, like, “Here’s what we’re trying to accomplish, here’s how the different pieces fit together.” And when a new thing happens, you know, “OK, this fits into the plan,” or, “This doesn’t fit into the plan; we need to make a course correction.”

And right now, AI is just not at all capable of that. And I think one of the big questions is: Is that going to change?

So, there’s an organization called METR that made a chart that’s become famous in the AI world that — about the task length. So what they do is they — this is for programming tasks, but it seems to work for other things — they estimate how long would it take a human being to do this task, and then they look at what length of task is AI able to complete with better than 50% accuracy. And that’s been going up at a pretty steady rate.

And so, many programming tasks that take a few hours now, an AI model can do. And if that continues, you could get to a point where AI models can do jobs that take a few days or a few weeks. And you could really start to think, “OK, maybe we’re going to make a lot of people obsolete.”

The thing that’s tricky, though, is that the kinds of tasks that AI models are good at are the kinds of tasks where you give the AI a really clear problem statement and you have a clear way of evaluating: Did it do it correctly? And most short tasks are like that. You say, “Fix this specific bug.” After you fix the bug, you can check that it was fixed correctly.

But over the course of months or years, what a software engineer has to do is pretty different. It’s like, “Optimize this website.” What does that mean? Well, you have to talk to customers, you have to do economic analysis. There’s other stuff you have to do where it’s actually, like, a different category of problem. And, I think that the current AI models, or the current way we train the AI models, just may not do that.

So, this paper looks at — I sort of often get questions from people about mixed-use zoning, commercial versus residential zoning. Like, “Do we need, like, YIMBYism for stores?” This kind of stuff.

And because I write a lot about zoning, and I think in a large set of the history of talking about zoning, it’s this separation of uses has been what people are talking about, rather than the question of residential density in the residential zones.

I have always professed agnosticism about this question. That I personally enjoy mixed-use neighborhoods, but I don’t know that there’s an important policy reason to force people to allow a 7-Eleven in their neighborhood in the same way that there is to allow housing in their town.

But, so what these people do is they compare how businesses are sort of spatially allocated in American cities versus in Taipei, because Taipei, it’s, like, mixed-use zoning everywhere. And so, what they’re doing is they’re measuring, like, actually, like, how much mixing of uses would occur without the regulatory constraint. And they find that it’s a lot, right?

That, like, the spatial — the rules in the United States are significantly binding, they think, based on this analysis, and that it has some externalities justification, right? That you’re removing a certain number of nuisances. But you can tell by looking at prices and actual residential demand that mostly you are creating deadweight loss, and that there is a large welfare loss, they think, from single-use residential zoning in American cities, and that you could make people substantially better off by forcing them to allow 7-Elevens in all residential zones.

I think this will probably not be, like, an earth-shattering conclusion to, like, the joint Demsas-Yglesias audience, but, like, I had no, like, analytical basis for making this claim in the past other than, like, I grew up in Greenwich Village just like Jane Jacobs. Hahaha.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Now we have, like — I was complaining about her lack of real economics and math, and these guys have the economics and math to say that she’s correct.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah, I mean, this is one of those things where, like, when I think of a nice neighborhood, similarly to you, I’m like, I would like there to be, like, a corner store. Like, I would like to be able to, like, walk to a coffee shop. Like, I think it would be nice to be able to have, like, a grocery store within walking distance and a park and, like, whatever.

And, like, this kind of, like, mixed-use sense of a neighborhood is actually, I think, not what the quote-unquote “good life” was largely depicted as, which is, like, single-family home neighborhood. Maybe there’s a park, but there’s, like — you would have to get in your car and drive to get to, like, this other place, which is this sort of, you know, that has the shops, and another place where it has schools, or, like, whatever it is, and another place where you go to work.

And this kind of, like, Euclidean zoning is, you know, what it’s referred to as — like, this kind of separation of uses — is a big critique that, like, YIMBYs have leveled against, like, American zoning for a while. And, like, this paper indicates that there’s, like, huge welfare gains to be made if you were to just, like, chill out about that.

But, like, there’s, like, also, like, a secondary kind of finding in the paper, which is that, actually kind of, like, the Jacobsonian, like, Jane Jacobsonian view is actually more, explains a lot more of the variation than the Euclidean one, which I found kind of confusing.

So, like, the net effect of American zoning is more segregation, not less. But you still see that, like, somewhere between 5 to 31% of zoning decisions are trying to get towards mixing. So it’s, like, there’s this weird thing happening where, like, at, like, a baseline, there’s a ton of separation that exists of the uses. But then, like, a bunch of, like, planners have kind of bought into the Jane Jacobs kind of view and are attempting, on the margins, to move towards more mixed use.

And I think anyone looking at even, you know, new suburbs today, depending on where you are in the country — I think in Atlanta and I think in Texas you don’t see this as much — but I think when you look, it’s particularly in, I mean, the Virginia suburbs, which I’m, like, really familiar with, but also suburbs in the Midwest, millennial tastes for suburban living are much more mixed use than, like, their parents’ generation actually lived in.

So, if you go to, like, the suburbs in Virginia, where you see, like, a huge boom of residential development but also, like, a big data center boom, etc. — it’s, like, a big growing area of the country — you see, like, there are these, like, subdivisions of homes, but then, like, also, like, there’s, like, a Main Street with, like, five apartments. And then people will all, like, drive to the Main Street and then, like, walk around and, like, experience, like, some level of, like, mixed-use development. And, like, I’m not sure if I’d [say] that that’s net positive, but I do think that developers are recognizing a latent human or millennial taste, at least — or youthful taste — for more walkable environments.

Matthew Yglesias: I sort of have an interesting counterpoint to this whole discourse that I notice a lot here in Maine, where I am right now, is that I think everybody agrees that the small historic downtowns of Maine cities — whether it’s, like, Bangor or Belfast, whatever it is — where, you know, these are little towns that were built before there were cars, sometimes at a river, sometimes at a train stop, whatever, that, like, those are really nice compared to, like, a strip mall with a giant parking lot outside of it. And there’s a lot of sort of planning interest in, like, forcing commercial development to be in the downtowns, because the downtowns are nice and people want them to be vibrant.

But then, like, in practice, when you’re deciding where to go to, like, eat a meal, you know, like, in the moment, the fact that the place outside of town with the big parking lot, you’re sure you’re going to be able to park, whereas if you drive downtown, it’s, like, hard to say.

Or you want to open a grocery store. And you could open a little grocery store downtown, and it would be adorable. And as a tourist visiting for the weekend, you’d love to walk in and browse and feel guilty, and you’ll buy something.

But for workaday shopping, it’s just better for the supermarket to be really large. And to have a really large supermarket, it’s easier to go where the land is cheapest, and then you have a big parking lot, right? And so there’s this kind of not residential sprawl, but, like, commerce sprawl that, like, is universally acknowledged to be not as nice as everything being in a cutesy downtown, but it just kind of, like, meets the practical, you know, demand for parking and for stores to be big and to have a lot of inventory.

And I wonder — I always wonder, I mean, I — because I hate to become, like, on the side of more central planning of land use. But I do wonder if there isn’t a race to the — like, a parking race to the bottom. Where for each business you can sort of maximize your interests by having parking be as convenient as possible. But when the whole town is like that, that’s worse than if it’s a kind of, like, a bustling center.

And you do see, as you were saying, in the Sunbelt, these kind of developments where there’s these Potemkin downtowns that actually don’t have nearly enough people living in them to support the commerce that’s there, but people kind of like it to exist, right, as, like, part of the thing.

Or in San Diego, I was walking around an apartment-heavy area, and there was all these retail vacancies. And I asked a developer, I was like, “What’s going on?” And he’s like, “Well, by law, we have to have ground floor retail in all of these buildings, but the buildings are, like, eight stories tall, so they can, you know, build them with wood.” And he was like, “We — this would have to all be, like, 50-story apartment buildings that there isn’t demand for to, like, create the, like, ground floor mixed uses that people think they want.”

So, I don’t know.

Jerusalem Demsas: I mean, I do think — I mean, one of the things that this speaks to is just, like, how much housing policy can’t be extricated from, like, transit — transportation policy. Like, you could have, like, really amazing, like, mixed-use developments, but if they’re, like, not conveniently located to where dense populations already exist and it’s not, like, easy to get there, then you have to plan for, like, mass parking lots.

Like, the reason why in, like, New York City — like, one of the only places that’s, like, actually, like, largely traversed either via foot or via transit, public transit — you can have a bunch of, like, these grocery stores, and it, like, makes a lot of sense for them to have, like, no parking or whatever, is, like, people are getting there on foot or on bike or on train or whatever it is, or on bus.

And, like, it’s really, really difficult to just, like, force that from above, even with, like, good, I think, zoning policy, because it, like, requires a shift in how people are moving around the city.

And, like, you know, I’ve talked about Philadelphia on the show before. My sister lives in Philadelphia. I love Philadelphia — great city. And, like, one thing that’s great about it is, like — and this is true of, like, you know, most old cities you go to — if you’re, like, if they’re developed pre-automobile, like, Philadelphia still has, like — and even in these, like, very residential areas — like, these corner stores that are available for buying random convenience items, or there’s bars, or there’s coffee shops, like, in, like, very residential parts of Philadelphia. Like, you still have that, that are, like, walkable to most people who are buying these, like, you know, row houses and townhomes.

And that sort of thing is, like — it’s just, like, very, very difficult to develop a city in the way that people like to visit. I mean, there’s a classic joke, like, Americans go to Europe to walk around towns and neighborhoods that they themselves have disallowed to exist in their own cities. And, like, yeah, like, I agree with that.

And it will require, like, us to, like, do a — I mean, I agree, like, there’s a lot of — you have to do central planning when it comes to transportation. Like, there’s, like, no way not to have central planning when it comes to transportation. But that also implicates housing policy too, and zoning, which is, like, not just this question of, like, how many homes can you build, but, like, what is the form of the city that you’re trying to create?

Matthew Yglesias: But, you know, D.C., where we live, is pretty Philadelphia-like in its basic built environment, but does not have nearly as many corner stores and neighborhood bars and things like that. I guess D.C. certainly is a fairly dense, fairly walking — you know, walk, bike, transit have a high mode share — but that is very committed to, like, corridor zoning of commerce, you know.

And, like, you can really see, like, in Logan Circle, Shaw, U Street, where I live, that it’s, like, 14th Street, 7th Street, P Street, U Street — those have stores on them, and they form, like, a box. And then inside the box there’s no stores. And there’s the coffee bar on S and 11th, which is, like, grandfathered in. And everybody, it seems to — that everybody loves the random nonconforming neighborhood coffee shop. But when Harriet Tregoning, like a million years ago, she proposed…

Jerusalem Demsas: Who is that?

Matthew Yglesias: She was a planning director and then she worked for Obama.

Jerusalem Demsas: You can’t just, like, drop a name like that. Like anyone knows who that is.

Matthew Yglesias: Sorry. She was the D.C. planning director, and then she worked in the Obama administration at HUD, I think, or maybe DGS.

So, like, she had this proposal to, like, legalize corner stores, and I was like, “All right, like, everybody’s gonna love this. Like, this isn’t gonna be some, like, nightmare zoning battle.” And it turned into a nightmare zoning battle. And some very small change was made to, I think, just, like, make it easier for the grandfathered locations, you know, to stay in or, like, change their mode of business operation. And it really puzzled me. Like, I didn’t…

Jerusalem Demsas: Old people hate noise. I mean, that’s the biggest problem, you know? I mean, they really hate noise. Like, there’s, like, this great bar called — now we’re deep into D.C. living. So for our non-D.C.ers, you have to come visit Washington.

But I, you know, like, there’s this bar called — now I don’t remember what it is, but there’s this great bar in Shaw. And, like, at 10 p.m. — I mean, it’s in Shaw, it’s a very, like, vibrant neighborhood, there’s a lot of young people there. It’s one of the only outdoor bars right there. And, like, you know, we — you sit outside, and, like, at 10 p.m. they come and they, like, make everyone come inside because, like…

Matthew Yglesias: All Souls?

Jerusalem Demsas: All Souls, yes, exactly. They make everyone come inside because it’s, like, the, like, the neighbors will complain about noise. And this is not, like, a raucous even really establishment, but I just think that, like, noise is, like, the underrated problem for getting commercial ventures into residential areas.

Even though people like them during the day, they just want them to be coffee shops so that they don’t, like, bother them at night, you know?

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah, I mean, people need to find out, like, you can get really good white noise machines these days for your bedroom purposes. Like, there’s a lot of good stuff happening in the audio space. I don’t know.

You know, it’s — I’ve never — there was that article in The Atlantic about how, like…

Jerusalem Demsas: Oh God, don’t do this to me.

Matthew Yglesias: …about how, like, it’s racist to want it to be quiet or something. And as a white person who doesn’t mind the noise that much, I both…

Jerusalem Demsas: I love when you shift between being a white person and being a Latino person.

Matthew Yglesias: Well, this is maybe my Latinx roots. I mean, I don’t know. I read that article, and I was both like, I sort of agree with her that, like, people are, like, too worried about noise.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: But I don’t know that I agree with, like, the racial or class analysis of this. I think it is maybe just, like, I grew up on a loud street, and so, I don’t know, it seems fine to me.

Jerusalem Demsas: I will just note that there are many, many ethnicities out there, and some of them come from cultures where loudness is normal and some of them do not, but I do not think it falls cleanly on white versus non-white lines. That’s the only thing I’ll say about that article.

Matthew Yglesias: I don’t know. I mean…

Jerusalem Demsas: Are there quiet cultures that aren’t white? Like, you know, the 5 billion — 5 billion people exist.

Matthew Yglesias: I thought it was a rare media — just, like, exploring differential preferences, like, just, like, noise aversion. Because, as you say, it’s, like, it’s a really big deal in public policy.

You know, like, people’s preferences differ, obviously, and, like, that’s fine. But that’s what, like, goes back to this paper, right? Like, I think the implication of this paper is that whether it’s preference for quiet or whatever it is, that people imposing that via Euclidean zoning actually has, like, quite large deleterious economic impacts that are, like, broadly similar in scope to, like, anti-apartment paranoia.

Which was not obviously true to me — versus just, like, I disagree. It’s good to see that, like, not only are my preferences my preferences, but accommodating my preferences would have widespread benefits for all of humanity.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah, well, we love papers confirming priors.

Matthew Yglesias: That’s the kind of empirical research I like, you know?

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah. If you guys have papers out there that are confirming Matt’s and my priors, send them to us and maybe we’ll use them on Peer Review. But otherwise, Matt, this was great. I’ll see you next week.

Matthew Yglesias: Farewell.
