The end of an era for China's economy

Zhu Rongji's formula won't work anymore. But that doesn't mean Xi Jinping's will work either.

Noah Smith
Aug 16
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

Zhu Rongji has passed away at the age of 97. He was not the only architect of the economic reforms that have made China a modern powerhouse — Deng Xiaoping, Zhou Enlai, Chen Yun, and others were all important — but Zhu was perhaps the most skilled, versatile, and far-sighted. He presided over China’s greatest era of reform and opening up — 1991 to 2003 — and handled both macroeconomic and microeconomic policy with a skill that perhaps no other Chinese leader has ever matched.

In many ways, Zhu was the man who really made China a capitalist country. The privatization of state-owned enterprises had begun earlier, but Zhu continued and accelerated it. He was the main champion of China’s successful drive to join the WTO, which supercharged China’s export industries and led to a massive wave of foreign investment; he also engaged in a deregulation program to lure foreign businesses to manufacture things in China.

When the Asian financial crisis of 1997 led to a wave of bad loans, Zhu bailed out the banks, and growth quickly resumed. And Zhu also devised the most important tax reform in China’s modern history, transferring large amounts of local government revenue to the central government, while simultaneously letting local governments do things like borrow more money and sell more leases on land to fund their own activities.

There is no question in my mind that Zhu ought to be remembered as one of history’s great heroes. When he entered office, East Asia had 1.22 billion people living on less than $3 a day (in 2021 dollars) — more than half the world’s total. By the time Xi Jinping became China’s top leader, that number was one-sixth of what it had been:

This is the biggest and fastest decrease in absolute poverty that the human race has ever seen. Zhu didn’t do it alone, of course, but the economic model he devised was so effective at generating rapid growth that he deserves more credit than perhaps any individual other than Deng Xiaoping. The list of people who have done more to decrease aggregate human suffering is short indeed.

China is no longer the growth powerhouse it was in those earlier years. According to official statistics, over the last 15 years, China’s growth rate has fallen to 5% — less than half of what it was in Zhu’s time:

Some independent estimates put the growth rate much lower — maybe 2-3%. China is going through a difficult economic time right now, and its leaders have a tradition of “smoothing” official numbers by understating growth during booms and overstating it during busts.

Some amount of slowdown is to be expected. China is a much richer country than it was when Zhu left office — maybe five times richer. When Zhu ended his historic tenure in 2003, China was about as rich as Tanzania or Zambia is now. Today, it’s closer to Argentina or the Dominican Republic. A country can’t keep growing at supercharged rates forever; eventually, technological catch-up and capital deepening run their course, and a country is forced to grow based more on innovation and improved efficiency.

To be fair, Xi Jinping has taken some serious steps toward making that transition. His government has designed a “new national system” of research and development that tries to coordinate the entire supply chain of innovation, all the way from government-funded research labs to private companies putting products on the shelves. He has unleashed the most expensive and extensive system of industrial subsidies in world history, promoting essentially every advanced manufacturing industry in existence, as well as AI. These policies may be unorthodox, but their goal is the right one — they’re aimed at pushing China past middle-income status by replacing catch-up growth with frontier innovation.

Whether Xi’s policies have been effective at this goal is less clear. There’s actually a big debate over whether Chinese total factor productivity — a measure of overall economic efficiency — grew in the 2010s. The Penn World Tables, which had until recently shown a severe slowdown in TFP growth, recently changed their assumptions and now report very healthy annualized growth of over 2% throughout the 2010s. Other sources, such as the Conference Board and Brandt et al. (2022), still think there was a slowdown, and peg the rate at around 1%. But everyone agrees that China’s TFP growth has been slowing over time, and that Xi’s “industrial policy for everything” hasn’t managed to re-accelerate it so far.¹

In fact, a lot of people are noting that China now appears to have a “two-speed” or “k-shaped” economy — split between a high-tech manufacturing sector that’s increasingly the envy of the world, and a broader economy that’s still mired in the aftermath of the country’s epic real estate bust.

Here’s the WSJ:

At a factory so big it could fit dozens of football fields, Chinese furniture manufacturer DeRucci churns out up to 5,000 mattresses a day…Overseas sales grew 67% in 2025…But domestic sales, the bulk of DeRucci’s business, are shrinking amid a yearslong real-estate downturn in China…DeRucci’s revenue from China fell 8.8% last year and it expects overall profits to fall roughly 40% in the first half of 2026…

This is the split-screen reality of China’s economy. On the one hand: soaring exports, advanced manufacturing and cutting-edge technology. On the other: a shrinking labor market, tepid consumer spending and a real estate slump with no end in sight…Tepid domestic spending means that many Chinese companies have lowered prices, squeezing profits and forcing them into cost-cutting mode.

China is making a lot of stuff, but it’s not providing its people with a lot of good jobs that they could use to buy the stuff:

Li Daokui, a Chinese economist and professor at Tsinghua University, recently estimated that China’s broad unemployment rate is actually 10.2%, when factoring in people excluded from official statistics who have been unable to find work for at least two years…The number of people in China with flexible employment—work without a permanent contract—is expected to grow to 320 million in 2026, accounting for more than 40% of urban employment, according to think tank China New Employment Forms Research Center.

Yes, you read that right — by some estimates, gig work is now 40% of employment in Chinese cities. Here’s a longer Financial Times article on the same trend.

As a result, Chinese people are increasingly unable to afford the things China makes. You can see this in the slumping growth of retail sales in the years since the real estate bust began in 2022:

Industrial output in China is slowing as well — there’s a limit to how much Xi can push his country to produce — but retail sales are slowing much faster and may even soon start to shrink:

The clearest example of this is the auto industry. After decades of failing to catch up to developed countries in internal combustion cars, China took advantage of the battery revolution and its strength in electronics manufacturing to leapfrog internal combustion entirely, driving a massive EV export boom. But Chinese people aren’t buying those cars — domestic auto sales, even of EVs, have been falling since mid-2025:

Again and again, we see the same pattern — Chinese companies, encouraged by ultra-cheap bank loans and subsidies, manufacture enormous amounts of stuff, but even after the brutal price wars that result from this “involution”, Chinese consumers aren’t able or willing to increase their consumption. So Chinese manufacturers, desperate to recoup some of their costs, dump the resulting output in foreign markets for cut-rate prices.²

As many commentators have pointed out, this is a major cause of the “Second China Shock” — the wave of ultra-cheap high-tech Chinese manufacturing exports that is now threatening to forcibly de-industrialize Europe and some other parts of the world. If you’re China, you might not particularly care — risking (probably toothless) European ire might seem like a small price to pay for saving domestic growth from a real-estate-induced slump. Under Zhu Rongji, China exported its way to prosperity; why can’t Xi just repeat the feat now?

But there’s a huge difference between the 2000s and the 2020s. China’s economy has grown enormously since then, to the point where export markets can’t provide nearly the growth engine that they did in earlier decades. In the decade after Zhu got China into the WTO, it really was an export-driven economy. But it hasn’t really been one in a while:

In 2006, exporting 35% of China’s GDP meant exporting almost $1 trillion. In 2025, exporting only 21% of China’s GDP meant exporting around $4 trillion. There is just a limit to how much foreigners are going to pay for Chinese goods. And that means there’s a limit to how much Xi can revive the modern Chinese economy by exporting overcapacity.

This isn’t because other countries will put up tariffs against Chinese goods (though that will also happen). It’s because of a much deeper principle in economics. “The overwhelming evidence that trade falls with distance” is one of the most robust empirical facts in the entire economic literature. No matter how mighty an export engine China is, domestic consumption is always going to be more important, especially because China is such a huge country.

You can see this very clearly in the car market. Despite the surge of exports, domestic sales are still more than twice as large, meaning that the modest recent fall in domestic car sales has been enough to cancel out the greatest auto export boom in human history:

Xi’s growth strategy also faces another headwind that Zhu’s didn’t. As countries grow, they tend to add manufacturing first, but at some point this tends to slow down, and they start adding services instead. One reason is that eventually, domestic consumers start getting more satisfied with the amount of material stuff they have, and start turning their desires toward services like health care, travel, entertainment, insurance, finance, and leisure activities.

Despite China’s reputation as the land of manufacturing, and despite Xi Jinping’s “industrial policy of everything”, this process is happening in China too:

And manufacturing’s share of employment tends to fall even more rapidly than its share of the economy as a whole, because automation in manufacturing is traditionally pretty easy compared to other sectors. Between 2013 and 2022, China lost 18 million manufacturing jobs:

So Xi is fighting an uphill battle that Zhu never had to fight. It was possible to propel Chinese growth to 10% in the 90s simply by getting companies to build a bunch of factories and pump out cheap electronics, toys, furniture, and clothing. Today, even turning China into a powerhouse of robotics, autos, machine tools, ships, etc. isn’t enough to swim against the inevitable tide of structural change.

So far, he doesn’t seem to be winning that fight. His unprecedented industrial policy has made China somewhat stronger in some technologies, and it has probably kept growth from collapsing even further, but it hasn’t accelerated TFP growth or provided broad-based employment for Chinese people. And eventually the big push will have to flag — already fixed-asset investment is stalling, even in manufacturing, and industrial loans are growing much more slowly.

Then what are Chinese policymakers supposed to do? Trying to create an updated version of the microeconomic model that Zhu Rongji created in the 90s and 00s will simply not work. But I think China’s current leaders could still learn from Zhu’s macroeconomic policies — specifically, his bank bailouts.

After the Asian Financial Crisis of 1997, China’s banks — who had lent a lot of money to inefficient state-owned enterprises — had a ton of bad debt on their books. This threatened to do what it usually does in the aftermath of financial crises — i.e., paralyze the financial system and cause a recession by choking off lending. Zhu created several “asset management companies” to take the bad debt off of banks’ hands and turn it into quasi-government debt. Eventually, China grew out of that debt, and it became a minuscule fraction of GDP:

Today, China faces an even bigger overhang of bad debt, as a legacy of the real estate crash. Banks are facing a bunch of nonperforming loans, this time generally from real-estate-related companies rather than state-owned enterprises. A lot of this bad debt is from local government financing vehicles — companies local governments created to get revenue from the real estate boom, which borrowed a lot of money from banks that they now can’t pay back.

An obvious Zhu-like move would be to have the government bail out both the banks and the LGFVs. Outside observers like Logan Wright have been urging this for a while. So has Li Daokui, an influential Chinese economist. This is from last year:

The central government should take on at least 20 trillion yuan ($2.8 trillion) worth of local sovereign debt, David Li Daokui, an economics professor at Tsinghua University and a regular adviser on policy to Beijing, said in an interview…To solve the [debt] problem, Li proposed that the central government sell more bonds and use the proceeds to buy regional authorities’ debt. Provincial and municipal agencies could transfer assets to Beijing in exchange, he said…A swap at a scale of 20 to 50 trillion yuan would be effective in relieving debt burdens around the country[.]

For reference, 50 trillion yuan is about $7.4 trillion. This would be roughly comparable to the amount the U.S. spent on various bailouts after its real-estate-driven financial crisis in 2008. Those American bailouts weren’t popular, but in economic terms they were remarkably successful, stabilizing the financial system while ultimately costing the government little in the long run.

In the short term, government debt would go up. 50 trillion yuan is about 35% of China’s GDP; if all of the debt went onto the central government’s balance sheet, it would make China’s gross national debt about as large as Italy’s relative to the size of its economy, and a little bit larger than America’s. That’s a relatively modest increase, all told — and one that might get at least partially reversed later, as the Chinese economy recovers and some bad loans become good ones.

And bailouts would probably help resuscitate Chinese growth, by boosting aggregate demand. Here are translated excerpts from one of Li Daokui’s recent speeches:

My first core point is this: the biggest problem facing China’s macroeconomy today is not K-shaped divergence, but that the economy as a whole is running cold…[O]nce we start talking about K-shaped divergence, it is as though we are placing our hopes on the upward arm of the K and expecting it to pull the entire Chinese economy forward…[T]he upper arm of the K cannot pull up the entire economic base…

[T]he single biggest factor behind the excessively cold operation of China’s economy is still local government…[O]ver the past 20 years, local governments on average absorbed resources equivalent to 41 percent of GDP. The problem today is that local governments have become the principal blockage in the economy’s circulation...[T]he money borrowed by local governments circulates largely within the financial system, as new borrowing is used to repay old debt. This is the “blockage” visible in the financial dimension of the economy.

He’s talking about a balance sheet recession. Local governments and their LGFVs are so focused on repaying their bubble-era debts, Li argues, that they suck up a bunch of capital from the rest of the economy. Local governments are also in a position to distort the rest of the economy, by setting policy that maximizes revenue while hurting growth:

[L]ocal governments are seeking money from companies in every possible way: clawing back previously promised tax concessions, collecting taxes in advance, and so on…[L]ocal governments have become “heat absorbers” and energy “black holes.” This is the fundamental reason the economy is running cold.

The solution that Li proposes is to use central government money to bail out the local governments, so they can get back to being engines of economic demand:

The answer is therefore obvious: the central government, and indeed the public sector as a whole, should expand its debt level…The central government should issue more debt…The money could be used to stabilize real estate, invest in people, strengthen livelihood spending, or support local consumption subsidies…The problem today is that local governments do not have sufficient capacity to drive the economy.

This seems like the kind of plan Zhu Rongji might have enacted. Zhu was a remarkable figure — able to craft a stupendously successful new microeconomic growth model for China while simultaneously crafting wise macroeconomic policies to prevent bad debt and financial crises from derailing the whole thing.

Xi Jinping, in contrast, seems to think only in terms of microeconomics. He’s obsessed with industrial policy, while ignoring the macroeconomic factors that are making his policies far less effective. He should be listening to people like Li Daokui, who embody the legacy of Zhu’s technocratic approach. But that age is over, and the voices of wisdom in China’s system are often marginalized.

Imagine an alternate history where Herbert Hoover got reelected in 1933. The “great engineer” might have resisted the kind of demand-boosting measures that became a hallmark of Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal. The U.S. might have lingered longer in the depths of the Depression.

China, sadly, doesn’t have elections. When a Hoover comes along, the Chinese people are stuck; they can’t throw him out in favor of a Roosevelt. China has to wait and hope it gets lucky, with wise technocratic leaders like Zhu Rongji and Deng Xiaoping. In the 80s and 90s they hit the jackpot. Recently, not so much.

Share

1

The Conference Board forecasts a very slight acceleration to 1.1% in 2025, compared to their estimate of 0.9% in the 2010s. The PWT sees a decline from 2.48% in the 2010s to 1.84% in 2023.

2

This can help explain why Xi’s industrial policy hasn’t raised productivity growth. Even if companies get much better at the technology of making cars, people have to want to pay for those cars in order for them to represent real economic value.

Demography, Deportations and the Trump Stall

Why the American jobs machine is sputtering

Paul Krugman
Aug 16
∙
Preview
 
READ IN APP
 

Chart 1

Regardless of its other problems, the U.S. economy has always been a powerful engine of job creation. The 1970s, for example, were a time of stagflation and deep pessimism. Nonetheless, the nation gained almost 20 million jobs over the course of that decade.

Since Donald Trump returned to the White House, however, job growth has slowed to a crawl. Granted, it’s nothing like the plunge in employment that took place in 2020, as Covid shut much of the economy down. And a couple of strong job reports earlier this year encouraged some observers to believe that the worst of the Trump II job drought might be over.

But the most recent Employment Situation report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics estimated that employment actually fell in July, while simultaneously revising the estimates for earlier months down. Thus July’s report confirmed the now widespread view among economists that the Trump-era job slowdown isn’t a blip. It’s now clear that America has entered a new, possibly permanent era of stagnant employment.

Why is this happening? And why does it matter? As I’ll explain in this primer, long-run job creation is driven by growth in the supply of labor. U.S. labor supply growth has been slowing for some time, because Baby Boomers have been aging out of the work force. However, the rate of job growth has suddenly fallen further due to Trump’s harsh crackdown on immigrants. So it’s fair to call the onset of America’s current employment stagnation the “Trump Stall”.

Is this slowdown in employment growth necessarily a bad thing? There are fewer U.S. jobs than past trends would have predicted, but there are also fewer workers seeking jobs. So why is this a problem?

Well, it is indeed a problem. One reason is that America’s responsibilities — to ensure national security, to take care of retirees, maintain public infrastructure and provide healthcare — remain the same, but there will now be fewer workers, paying less taxes, than previously expected to meet those responsibilities. Moreover, foreign-born workers bring distinct skills and are willing to do jobs native-born workers shun, such as emptying bedpans and picking fruit. Removing them from the U.S. economy will leave the rest of us poorer and with a lower quality of life.

So for both the short run and the long run welfare of Americans, it’s important to understand the origins and consequences of the stalling of the American job machine. Beyond the paywall I will address the following:

1. Measuring the Trump Stall

2. The long-run drivers of job growth

3. Understanding the Trump Stall

4. Why the Trump Stall is harmful

5. The Trump Stall in context...

The Misery Will Continue Until Morale Improves

Why Trump is eviscerating the military

Paul Krugman
Aug 17
 
READ IN APP
 

According to an old military maxim, amateurs talk about strategy, professionals talk about logistics. But these days we need a third category: Immature, insecure guys think that war is about acting tough and looking cool.

Hi, Paul Krugman with a podcast update for today. I want to weigh in on the incredible rash of stories about how Trump and company are eviscerating the military. It is truly remarkable. If there’s one thing that we thought that the United States was still kind of number one at, it was that we had the world’s premier military. Now, of course, we managed to rather quickly effectively lose the war with Iran, although current management will never admit it.

But also just a series of stories, some of them related to that war, some of them going beyond and to other areas that just are truly shocking, even for somebody like me, who had no expectation that this administration would be doing any good for the nation.

Just to remember the story: So first we had the big warning that the U.S. military was basically running out of ammunition. That the precision missiles that are so essential to waging war were largely gone, expended unproductively against Iran. And clearly the cost benefit calculus was a disaster because the Iranians were sending cheap drones and we were using multi-million dollar weapons in an attempt to counter them.

After that, we got the story about the horrific conditions on board the USS Lincoln, the aircraft carrier that’s been stationed for a very long time without, it appears, adequate resupply and with toilets flooding. Apparently just horrific conditions, which turn out to be not unique to that ship: Other ships are having problems. There’s the USS Boxer, an amphibious assault ship, which apparently has run out of feminine hygiene products, among other things.

Okay, so we have those horrific stories. And then we have the stories about Trump intervening. Demanding, first, that the Navy construct a whole new class of ships, Trump-class battleships, which are useless and would be sitting ducks. Then demanding that the Navy replace modern catapults with steam catapults, which he thinks are cooler. And then demanding that they relocate the command tower on aircraft carriers because he wants them to look more like the way they looked during World War II.

Is this America? I mean, think about the American way of war. We are not a warrior nation, which is fine. We are a lot of other things.

We were a nation that was supreme in the arts of peace. We were a nation of know-how. America won its wars by doing the arts of peace right, by.building better and more stuff than other countries. By getting our act together in ways that didn’t necessarily involve fighting.

Of course, you always need courageous warriors. You always need people able and willing to risk death in the service of their nation. But what America was supreme at was logistics. If you ask how did America and its allies pull off D-Day, well, a lot of it was being able to deliver supplies to the beaches of Normandy in a way that the Germans never thought was possible.

America was always the place, the country that was really good at logistics. For us to be not feeding our sailors, not able to keep ships that are not, after all, under fire all the time, to keep the plumbing working, that is incredible.

The idea that the president is imposing his personal aesthetic preferences to undo design decisions that were made by military professionals is also basically incredible.

Okay, what is this all about? And what happened? Some of it is specifically military, but mostly it’s not. I think these military failings should be put in the same context as the frantic and disastrous destruction and redesign of Washington, D.C. The demolition of the East Wing. The disastrous attempt to refurbish the reflecting pool to reflect Trump’s aesthetics. Even the gold leaf and gold lettering that is polluting the White House. All of this is really part of the same picture.So what is going on here?

Obviously we have a seriously mentally ill, mentally deficient guy with his finger on the button. The president of the United States is clearly dissociating, I’ve been calling it sundowning because I personally saw sundowning during my father’s awful last year.

Trump is not in full possession of his faculties, and he is obsessing about things that are really just kind of remnant ego trips. I haven’t read the Haberman book yet, but reportedly he spends a large fraction of his time and probably a larger fraction of his mental energy on his redecoration projects, which aside from all being carried out disastrously are also in incredibly bad taste. But this is where he is. He’s actually more interested in his giant, tacky, gilded ballroom than he is in the fate of the nation.

But how does somebody like this end up able to impose his will on these disastrous things? How does he end up able to eviscerate the military?

Well, part of it is that this is a wannabe authoritarian regime. We’re in a peculiar state now where the United States is not yet a police state. It is not yet a place where the secret police will cart you away for expressing the wrong opinion, unless you are not a white U.S. citizen. Maybe the time is coming when that will happen. But in any case, we are not yet East Germany under the Stasi. We are not yet Putin’s Russia.

But the Republican Party, senior politicians, who should be feeling that they have at least some dignity, ability to take a stand, behave as if they were living in an authoritarian state. They’re obviously terrified. They’re afraid to express any dissent. They go along with Bush’s — see, I’m dissociating, living in the past myself. They’re going along with Trump’s wishes.

On top of that, I think it really helps to think of the ruling party in America right now as being a party that behaves as if we were a full-on authoritarian state. And one of the things we learn about in studying how authoritarian regimes behave is, first of all, that the leader actually can be possibly the worst informed person in the nation because nobody dares to tell him bad news. We’re hearing this a lot about Putin, that he doesn’t know how badly his war is going. Well, Trump in many ways probably still doesn’t understand how badly his war is going.

The really striking thing about the munitions shortage and now the horrible conditions on US ships is that to the extent that any action has been taken on either of those issues is it has been only after extensive reporting in the press. So now the Pentagon is talking about a crash program to have defense manufacturers produce more of the missiles that we’ve been running out of. But it’s not clear it’s even started yet, and that call didn’t happen until many months into the war, whereas the munition shortage was obvious to independent observers just a few weeks in — that we were expending munitions that we couldn’t replace. Nothing happened until there was widespread press reporting.

The USS Lincoln has finally been recalled for refit and shore leave. But that didn’t happen until after many press stories about it, all of which were denied, but it’s very obvious just looking at the behavior that the Pentagon and Hegseth and Trump finally reacted saying, oh, I guess something needs to be done. We can’t let this go on. But they didn’t do it until after the press reported.

Now, is this because they’re totally callous? Well, they are. They don’t care at all. The people who yell support the troops most loudly are the people who actually have no interest whatsoever in supporting the troops. But I think it’s probably also the case that they may not have known. That nobody told Trump that we were running out of missiles. He may have read some press stories to that effect, but he said that’s all fake news and nobody within the administration was willing to tell him.

They may not have been willing to tell Hegseth either, who by all accounts flies into a rage and punishes anybody who brings him bad news.So they just didn’t hear about this. They didn’t hear about the munitions. They didn’t hear about the conditions for US sailors until the drumbeat fromthe press became too loud for them to remain insulated, to remain in denial.

So this is what happens. This is the problem with authoritarian regimes. It goes with the related problem with authoritarian regimes, which is that they have a single point of failure. You elevate one person to a position of untouchable authority, and if that person loses it, that person is sundowning, there is no recourse.

One more thing to say about what’s going on is that authoritarian regimes systematically promote incompetence. This is Hannah Arendt on totalitarianism. That it’s not just that they value loyalty above competence. They actually actively dislike competence. Because someone who is competent, someone who knows what they’re doing, might stand on their dignity, might refuse to follow instructions from above. You need third-raters or worse.

This has long been true in areas that I know something about. It’s been true of right-wing economics forever. It’s long been the case that although there are plenty of conservative, competent economists, what the right-wing wanted, even pre-Trump, was creatures like Steve Moore or Larry Kudlow, people who had no idea actually how to do economic analysis, but were unimpeachably, unquestionably loyal because after all, they had no constituency to fall back on.

So we have this mix of leader principle, Führerprinzip. Yes, I think we’re allowed to use the original German here. Information blackout at the top because nobody wants to tell the leader bad news. And incompetence as a general principle throughout the government.

And if you want to understand how the Reflecting Pool happened, if you want to understand how we ended up with this hole in the ground, that was previously the east wing of the White House, all of this is fundamentally the same stuff and it’s true of lots of other areas of policy as well.

Still, I guess most of us thought — I thought, mea culpa — that the military would be among the last places to be hit by this. That, first of all, it should be obvious even to people likeTrump and Hegseth that you don’t muck too much with the military, that you don’t destroy the one instrument you really have, and also that the military itself had, so I thought, a strong enough culture, was highly enough respected among the populace that the military would be able to stand up and say no.

But it turns out that I was wrong. And so instead of being insulated from the craziness and incompetence, the military is actually possibly the most acute victim of everything that’s happening.

At this point they might manage to start feeding the sailors and fix the toilets, though I wouldn’t put 100% odds on that. But the broader problem of really destroying one of the last real sources of U.S. strength, that is not going to go away. Instead, it’s going to be the same thing. And the misery will continue until morale improves.

Have a great day.

Woke 1 is dead. We’ve learned nothing.

Blatant indifference to facts is all too common across ideologies

Matthew Yglesias
Aug 17
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

I’m of two minds about the “Woke 1 was crazy” discourse.

  1. I agree with those who find this to be inadequately apologetic to the individuals whose lives and careers were unjustifiably upended.

  2. No one likes to admit that they were wrong about anything, and if this evasive formulation allows people to shift to new, better views, that’s good.

I’ll offer this Idrees Kahloon article in The Atlantic if you want a taste of (1), but there are lots of articles along those lines and, rather than chime in with one of my own, I want to make a different observation: Whatever you think Woke 1 was, it arose under structural conditions that are very much still with us and that extend well beyond the specific politics of the left.

Many of the themes that dominated Woke 1 discourse have died down. And institutional leaders, to their credit, have gotten a lot better at not reacting in a dysfunctional way to social-media outrage mobs.

But it’s still very much the case that in a world without strong gatekeepers, false or absurd ideas can spread like wildfire and become a kind of instant conventional wisdom.

And what I personally remember most bitterly about Woke 1 is not the behavior of the most hysterical people; it’s the behavior of the people who knew perfectly well that others were behaving hysterically and who carefully avoided saying false or insane things (that’s how you can know that they knew) but who also avoided actively contesting them.

This was, for the most part, savvy behavior.

Those who actually said nutty things have suffered for it to an extent, which is exactly why there’s now this effort to slink away from them. But those who ended up on the wrong side of Woke 1 fads also suffered. The winners were those who ducked the storm — budget experts who knew it wasn’t true that cities spend more money on police than schools but didn’t say so — and emerged with their reputations unscathed.

That incentive structure to avoid being the “well, actually” guy is still very much with us and means that any kind of discourse could go wildly off the rails. And unfortunately, while we are now deeply into an anti-woke backlash on the right, the backlash isn’t taking the form of resisting the poor epistemic practices of the woke left — it’s resisting the value of caring about the weak and unfortunate while replicating the same toxic dynamics.

It’s what it says about you

When Vox was launching, its first social-media staffer explained to me that the essence of social sharing is that it doesn’t really matter what the article says. What matters is what the act of sharing the article says about the sharer.

In the summer of 2020, sharing an anti-policing article signified “I think racism is bad.” So lots of people who, rightly, thought that racism was bad shared lots of anti-policing articles.

And lots of these articles made striking claims. Anyone in a calm, rational frame of mind would say that the right way to respond to an article making a striking and radical claim — that policing originated in slave patrols, that city budgets are dominated by policing, that there’s no evidence policing reduces crime, etc. — would be with a mix of curiosity and skepticism. Curiosity, because sometimes in life we learn something genuinely new that upsets our previously settled understanding of the world. But also skepticism, because it ought to be a little bit hard to shake off your views.

Twenty-first-century technology has, in theory, made it easier than ever to respond to novel claims with an appropriate mix of curiosity and skepticism. You can just look stuff up on your phone or laptop with incredible ease.

In practice, though, people mostly don’t do this. You just reshare the article because of what the act of resharing says about you.

Anti-policing articles are not currently getting a lot of shares, because in the summer of 2026 sharing anti-policing articles says something like “This guy is stuck in the past.” The progressive cause of the moment is Palestine, not anti-racism, so the specific habit of giving assent to wildly overblown factual claims to show you care has migrated from policing to Israel. That’s less practically harmful because it involves a small foreign country over which American progressives have very little actual influence rather than the governance of large American cities.

But a readily available structural dynamic that can easily shift to new topics can be utilized by all ideological camps.

Currents of right-wing hysteria

The ideological camps in America are never mirror images of each other, and one major contrast is a diffuse, fairly leaderless left against a right that is centered on the personality of Donald Trump.

So the ultimate taboo on the right today is not an emergent social-media phenomenon at all, but rather a top-down line about the 2020 presidential election. To get a presidential appointment, you need to be willing to at least pretend to believe that the 2020 election was stolen, and to participate in conservative politics at all, you need to say that this expectation is an unremarkable development and that anyone bothered by it is afflicted with some kind of irrational “Trump derangement syndrome.”

But this isn’t the only example of diffuse insanity on the right.

Another is the panic around vaccines and/or Tylenol being responsible for the rise in autism in America. This is the kind of “big, if true” claim that a rational person would respond to by looking into it. And I think it’s just really clear, if you bother to look into it, that neither vaccines nor Tylenol is responsible for the rise in autism diagnoses, because the rise in autism diagnoses is fully explained by a shift in the diagnostic criteria. There is no rise to explain. Nothing caused it.

Back in 2024 when Joe Biden was president and crime was falling from its pandemic-era peak, the internet was awash in conservative conspiracy theories about manipulation of the crime stats.

Now that Trump is president and crime has continued to fall, pretending to believe that crime is soaring has lost its instrumental value, so you don’t hear that anymore. You do, however, continue to see conservatives asserting without bothering to look it up that crime rates are lower in states like Texas and Florida than in New York and California.

Subscribed

We also go through these bizarre spasms of conservatives arguing that people were richer in the 1950s when, again, this is not a remotely hard claim to evaluate by just looking stuff up. There’s no need to belabor this endlessly, but we all know that if you tweet something inflammatory about immigrants, crime, sharia, the city of Chicago or ideally some combination of the above, then tons and tons of right-wing people will pay it forward without making the slightest effort to assess whether it’s true.

And we also know that the very people most likely to do this are exactly the people most likely to get mad at progressives for behaving the same way around a different “woke” set of topics.

We have to learn to care about facts

My official analysis is that this is fundamentally a structural, technologically driven phenomenon.

At the same time, I really don’t think it’s good to shrug at poor epistemic practices and just chalk it up to the nature of social media. It is in the nature of social media for people to behave that way. But that just means it’s incumbent on those of us with a high profile and some ability to steer the discourse to take time out of our busy days and try to lean against these trends.

I have incredible respect for Andy Masley’s tireless efforts to serve as a corrective against the tide of hysteria about data centers. What’s particularly impressive about his work on this topic is that he refuses to just flip to the other side and become a hardcore warrior on behalf of data centers. Some people say that the hysteria on this topic is a propaganda op led by the People’s Republic of China, but Masley looked into it and says there’s scant evidence for this. He also says that while most of the panic about data centers is misguided, there is a very real localized noise nuisance problem that’s easily addressable with appropriate setback rules but has not always been addressed effectively.

In terms of what it says about you, unfortunately, “data centers are underregulated in certain ways but not in others and while the companies building them are mostly getting a bad rap they are also spreading a false counter-conspiracy theory to try to get their way” just sort of positions you as an annoying, persnickety person.

Importantly, even though this is kind of my personality, I have learned over the years that this is not the way to behave in real life.

It is rude and annoying to start challenging friends and acquaintances on the casual assertions they make during a dinner party, asking for evidence, drawing fussy distinctions, etc. It can be fun and entertaining to have a back and forth about something, but, in person, you really do have to “read the room” to know whether that would be welcome or would kill the vibe.

That kind of social behavior tends to carry over into social media, which really is social in the sense of being dominated by cliques and in-group/out-group dynamics. But it’s dysfunctional in a social-media context because social media really is media, which ideally would be about helping people understand the world in a truthful way.

True wokeness requires knowledge

The good thing about “woke” behavior is that, in principle, the instinct to try to show that you care about the most vulnerable people is correct and praiseworthy.

The disaster of the anti-woke backlash is that instead of rebelling against the specific bad habits of the left, it has largely proceeded by attacking the value of caring about people. Rightists have started obsessively invoking concepts like “virtue signaling” and “suicidal empathy” to put forward a kind of atavistic selfishness as a personal ethic, often wallowing in cruelty.

But, truly, you ought to care about the suffering of others.

Caring is only worthwhile if you do things that are useful, though. People tend to appreciate this when it comes to matters that are close at hand. If you want to help your kid or your sister or friend, you need to find a way of providing assistance that actually works, not just go on vibes. And the reality is that public policy involves a lot of tedious technical minutiae. It’s totally reasonable that most people, most of the time, mostly don’t want to master the technical minutiae of public policy questions.

But if you don’t want to learn a lot of boring details about crime statistics or immigration trends or utility regulation or the Israel-Palestine conflict, then it would also make sense to avoid broadcasting strongly held opinions about these things.

Conversely, if you’re going to have well-grounded and strongly held views on an issue, ideally you’d do something about it.

Lots of progressives got, rightly, furious at the way DOGE disrupted some incredibly valuable global public-health programs. These programs are, dollar-for-dollar, the most effective ways of helping people. But I wish I saw equal passion for actually raising money for these kinds of causes or acknowledging their objective significance in contexts other than “being mad at Elon Musk.”

But beyond that, we’ve only identified highly effective public-health interventions after a lot of trial and error and failure both in the medical science and in the broader field of development and foreign aid. There’s a common view in left-wing and right-wing populisms that solving problems is very easy intellectually and you just need to defeat and disempower the bad people. This is not a view that would survive serious learning about the history of basically any policy topic.

It’s actually quite hard to learn what works and why and to implement good ideas at scale. The Woke 1 problems of dogmatism, incuriosity, closed-mindedness, and sloppiness about the facts are not solved by switching the focus from identity to economics or by becoming right-wing.

You need to actually behave less dogmatically, more curiously, more open-mindedly, and more rigorously, and I don’t see a lot of evidence that the discourse is moving in that direction.
