Two kinds of moderate Democrats

There are many pragmatists, but few have the courage to say what they really think.

Matthew Yglesias
Aug 19
 
READ IN APP
 

Yesterday, I wrote about the distinction between the Insurgent Left and the Progressive Establishment. Today, I want to continue trying to enrich people’s understanding of the Democratic Party factional landscape by drawing a distinction on the moderate side between Tactical Moderates and True Believers.

It can be a little hard to tell the difference because if you’re moderate for tactical reasons, you’re of course going to say that you’re a True Believer. And True Believers still believe in the tactical case for moderation and will make that case in an effort to gain support.

The distinction is often revealed only in the moment.

Abigail Spanberger had a somewhat moderate-ish profile as a House member from a blue-leaning purple district, and she ran for governor of Virginia on that profile and won. Virginia only allows governors to serve one term and is a solidly blue state on the federal level, so to whatever extent Spanberger has ambitions to become a senator or serve on a national ticket or in a cabinet, her incentive is to cater to the Progressive Establishment.

The fact that she is instead operating as a force of restraint against the Democratic legislature is thus a source of real frustration to a lot of Virginia Democrats. But I think she’s correct on the merits to raise doubts about mandating collective bargaining for local government employees.

When Sarah McBride went on “The Ezra Klein Show,” it seemed to me that she was trying to create space for a tactical retreat from an electorally indefensible line on trans women’s participation in competitive women’s sports. Martina Navratilova, by contrast, is trying to persuade Democrats that the left’s line on this is genuinely wrong.

I think that within reasonable bounds, tactical moderation is smart.

I do not agree with John Bel Edwards’s positions on guns or abortion, but it’s obviously the case that no candidate espousing progressive views on those topics would have won a gubernatorial election in Louisiana. It would’ve been great if he’d been persuaded to run for Senate. In general, I’d love to see Democrats nominate more politicians like that in the Deep South because it would create a chance to make progress on Medicaid expansion. Both parties’ decision to just write off huge swaths of the country as unwinnable is bad for America, and a renewed spirit of tactical moderation would bring real substantive benefits.

But I also think moderate Democrats are running on fumes in terms of what tactical moderation can accomplish. Expanding the tent in terms of red state recruiting is a totally reasonable agenda that I think even very left-wing people should see the merits of.

At the end of the day, though, if you want to capture the heart of the party, you need to make arguments that are grounded in conviction, and that means arguing on the merits.

Subscribed

The Joe Manchin paradox

Consider former Senator Joe Manchin of West Virginia. Everyone who wasn’t completely addled understood that Democrats were wildly lucky to have a West Virginia Senate seat and that there was no way a conventional progressive could have won the 2012 and 2018 Senate races there.

But I think most progressives felt that Manchin was clearly drawing dead in terms of re-election in 2024 and what they wanted him to do in 2021–22 was YOLO it and vote for filibuster abolition and a sweeping progressive agenda.

And that really is the logic of tactical moderation.

Harry Reid had an old joke about Susan Collins, saying she’ll always be with us except when we need her vote. And there’s clearly something to this. Collins cast a totally inconsequential but highly salient “no” vote on Amy Coney Barrett right before her 2020 re-election, but she cast a consequential vote in favor of Brett Kavanaugh and many lower court judges earlier. She’s criticized or broken with Trump on a number of issues but never really collaborated with Democrats to meaningfully restrain him and clearly maintains a sufficiently cordial relationship with the White House that unlike John Cornyn, she never faced a serious MAGA challenger.

But it’s also true that Collins provided decisive votes in favor of the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act in 2009, the Dodd-Frank Act in 2010, and against Affordable Care Act repeal in 2017.

There’s probably just no such thing as a politician who at heart agrees with the base about everything but is also good enough at faking moderation to repeatedly win races in tough states like West Virginia and Maine.

So while it’s certainly coherent to appreciate a Manchin-style figure on a purely tactical level without agreeing with him on anything, I think it’s unrealistic to expect that actual politicians are just totally faking it.

Among other things, once you start playing the role of “guy who champions the interests of coal communities against the demands of green groups,” you’ll come to realize that the green groups are genuinely wrong about some things. At the end of the day, I think environmentalists are basically right about coal. But no advocacy community is right about everything, and there’s plenty the climate movement gets wrong. Most elected officials are not incentivized to delve too deeply into the merits of policy or to really scrutinize their coalition partners’ demands. But a Democrat from West Virginia is incentivized to find things the Progressive Establishment is wrong about, so over and above anything tactical, he’s likely to find genuine points of disagreement.

Personally, I think Manchin was wrong on the merits about some important stuff (notably the filibuster) but also substantially correct that the Build Back Better legislation that congressional leadership was pushing for was inflationary. His push to make Democratic climate efforts more focused on innovation and clean energy deployment and less focused on blocking pipelines was right on the merits. The country would be better off today if Democrats had embraced his permitting legislation more fulsomely.

The True Believers

All the way at the other end of the spectrum, you have Representative Ed Case of Hawaii.

Case is a formidable electoral over-performer. In the Split Ticket database, he overperformed by 17 points in 2018, 14 points in 2020, 18 points in 2022, and 17 points in 2024. He’s been in and out of the Blue Dog caucus over some internecine disputes that I don’t really understand, but he generally has a moderate Blue Dog-ish record. He faced a primary challenge this cycle that, for example, slammed him for supporting the SAVE America Act.

The thing about this is that while Case’s vote-getting skills are impressive, there is genuinely no tactical case for having a moderate in this seat.

Kamala Harris won his district 62 to 37. Elizabeth Warren is, as Slow Boring readers know, an absolutely terrible electoral underperformer. It just doesn’t matter because she represents Massachusetts. But Harris did slightly worse in Massachusetts statewide than she did in Case’s district.

Case is moderate because it’s what he believes, not because it’s what he needs to believe to win his district. He’s also lost several statewide primaries — once for governor, twice for Senate — in part because the Democratic Party primary voters of Hawaii generally prefer someone more progressive. In that light, it’s actually pretty impressive that he fended off an insurgent challenger this cycle, and it’s notable that he had to do so based purely on arguing the merits with no real electability case to be made.

Case is truly a one of one in this regard.

But I have absolutely talked to members of Congress who’ve told me they secretly wish they had purple seats so they could mod-out a bit more and then plead electability when the groups give them shit for it. I think this is mostly a mix of lying and self-deception, but it contains a grain of truth. Most people — even people who would describe themselves as quite progressive — have an issue or two where they break from the pack. But vanishingly few safe-seat members are like this. You don’t see many guys in a D+7 seat who espouse an idiosyncratic moderate position on something unless it’s closely related to home state or district politics.

But plenty of people have a heterodoxy or two they’re quietly stifling. There are also plenty of members who like to engage in what I’ve termed “dog-whistle moderation” or maybe meta-moderation, where they’ll speak in abstract terms about the need to meet voters where they are and change the Democratic Party’s brand and not be held hostage to extremists.

Subscribed

These types tend to complain a lot about the Insurgent Left in a way that doesn’t totally make sense. Iowa didn’t flip from being an Obama-Obama state to a Trump-Trump-Trump state because of Bernie Sanders (who, after all, was in the caucus the whole time). It flipped because mainstream Democrats got more left-wing.

But if you want to change that, you need less obfuscation and more Ed Case energy.

Beyond “the establishment”

Mike Zapler wrote a piece for Axios this week titled “The Democratic Establishment’s Ideas Deficit” in which he argues that “centrists” know what they’re against but have a harder time defining what they’re for.

I think he made some good points but also repeats a fundamental conceptual confusion about this.

If by “the Democratic establishment” you mean something like “the party’s congressional leaders and its past few presidential nominees,” then the reason they have a hard time defining what centrist agenda they favor is that they do not favor a centrist agenda.

It’s actually not even slightly difficult to specify the policy priorities of the Biden-Harris administration as advanced in Congress by Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries. The Biden-Harris administration wanted to increase the tax revenue share of G.D.P. while making the tax code more progressive and to use the vast majority of that new revenue to increase spending on clean energy and social services. They believed in abortion rights and affirmative action in college admissions and a fairly crude approach to elite representational politics. On their watch, domestic oil-and-gas production reached new record levels but only after efforts to halt new leases were blocked in court. They believed in the neo-Brandeisian antitrust agenda and appointed its key leaders to top regulatory jobs.

The reason this agenda appears to be just “stuff progressives want, minus some of the stuff that progressives want” is because literally that’s what it is.

The establishment’s enthusiasm for progressive policy is tempered by electoral prudence, court losses, and leadership’s need to set priorities, but their agenda is genuinely a subset of the progressive agenda.

At the same time, an alternative centrist agenda is not hard to find or hard to understand. It would emphasize deficit reduction to put downward pressure on inflation and interest rates and prioritize clean energy abundance while championing domestic fossil-fuel production as superior to foreign production as long as demand for oil and gas exists. It would center ideas, like performance pay for teachers, that aim to increase the productivity of the public sector. It would be an agenda that balances the need for an inclusive economy with a healthy respect for the virtues of free markets and that takes seriously supply-side regulatory constraints on things like housing and health care. Add in the notions that crime control and border security are genuinely important state functions, not things to be engaged in reluctantly as a rearguard effort to avoid political harm.

These are not unfamiliar or secret ideas. They represent substantive moderation, a belief that the progressive NGO blob’s analysis of the major policy problems in American life is not really correct or adequate to the scale of the challenges the country is facing.

I understand why many moderate True Believers don’t want to be more assertive about these kinds of issues. They’re afraid of losing primaries to candidates to their left, and they think that articulating some loud and proud moderate positions is risky compared with minimizing the substantive differences and making a tactical case for moderation.

That analysis makes sense, to an extent, but I think that after 10 years of factional warfare, we can see that it’s a losing strategy for the long term. Nobody wins elections based on a pure politics of from-the-heart conviction. But opportunism and practicality can’t be your whole argument. Actually picking fights about important public-policy questions — not fights with the far left but fights with the establishment and the status quo — makes you seem more authentic and interesting. Picking these fights could also help push back against the sense that moderates practice an inherently dreary politics of limits and “no, you can’t do that.” I think there’s something genuinely inspiring about an agenda that uses abundant housing, rapid economic growth in blue states, and low crime to unlock new avenues of opportunity. It’s really shameful for New York and California to be worse at teaching kids to read than Mississippi, and it would be really amazing if the results achieved by their public school systems were commensurate with the resources invested.

The collective action problem around taking on the groups is real, but a presidential campaign could provide a good context for doing so.

Since moderates are better at winning votes, they’ll always have a tactical argument at their disposal. But I think there are a lot of closeted True Believers out there who right now are so afraid of losing to leftists that they forget to actually be different from the leftists they’re afraid of. That needs to change.

title: Economists should be worried about birth rates

Economists should be worried about birth rates

Don’t be so quick to dismiss the threat of an aging, declining population.

Noah Smith
Aug 19
 
READ IN APP
 

The Economist has an interesting article this week, in which it goes after Daron Acemoglu. Acemoglu is probably the top economist in the world at this point, having just earned a Nobel prize, and sitting right at the top of the list of most cited economists. So it’s kind of funny that when it talks about people who doubt Acemoglu’s research, the one person it mentions is…me!

Give an economist a few drinks, however, and some of them will venture their true opinions about this giant. “Much of his theoretical work is useful, but he uses his models to inform populist policies that have been tried before and failed,” blasts one well-known economist. Some commentators do not require Dutch courage. “I’ve been yelling about Acemoglu for literally a decade,” Noah Smith, an economics blogger, has said, in response to a flurry of online criticism of Mr Acemoglu’s work.

It is true that I have been pretty critical of much of Acemoglu’s work over the years. In 2012 I argued strongly against a paper he wrote in which he claimed that America is more entrepreneurial than Sweden because America’s weaker safety net forces people to work harder (in actuality, Sweden is more entrepreneurial by most measures). In 2022 I pointed out that a famous Acemoglu paper claiming that robots destroy jobs was actually an outlier, and listed a bunch of other papers that reach the opposite conclusion. I liked his book Why Nations Fail, but I also admit that its empirical foundations are fairly shaky. I didn’t like Acemoglu’s more recent book Power and Progress, and I was highly critical of a recent paper Acemoglu wrote about AI and productivity.

But this is hardly newsworthy. I go after Acemoglu’s work because I know he can take it; he’s a titan of the economics field, and I am but a lowly blogger. Nothing I say is going to affect his reputation or his prestige, even if someone at The Economist mentions my critiques in an article. Indeed, after the article came out, top figures in the profession rushed to condemn it and to defend Acemoglu. The Economist does list a bunch of — usually justified — criticisms of Acemoglu’s work, but this does not mean Acemoglu has been discredited as a researcher or exposed as overrated; indeed, it would be difficult to name a top economist whose body of work does not contain a variety of questionable theoretical assumptions, motivated reasoning, and/or shaky empirical results. This is a problem with the field itself, not the man; it’s part of a broader crisis of unreliability throughout much of academia.

But for that same reason, despite the Economist article’s lack of newsworthiness, I think it’s good that the magazine decided to come at the king. Economics is far too hierarchical and closed of a profession. Younger and less accomplished researchers routinely defer to the authority of famous and senior figures, and critics from outside the field are typically brushed off. Exactly how it got to be this way is a topic that deserves a longer post, but I believe the hierarchical, closed culture of econ has resulted in a research literature that has been too skewed toward the priorities and intuition of top authority figures. I thus think it’s generally a healthy thing to tweak the tails of those Olympian figures, as long as criticisms are grounded in substance. As they say, “science is the belief in the ignorance of experts.”

So in that spirit, let’s critique another Acemoglu paper.

First, the background. Recently, a lot of people (including myself, but also prominent economists) have begun worrying about low fertility rates. Across all countries — poor as well as rich — fertility just keeps going down and down, with no floor in sight.

This presents two distinct dangers: population aging and population shrinkage. Aging, rather mechanically, creates a burden for young people, because you have more retirees who have to be supported by each worker, either through taxes or through family support. It also might reduce productivity, for example if older managers are less innovative, but that’s more speculative. Population shrinkage, meanwhile, is a threat to total GDP, which you might care about if you want your country to be more powerful. There’s also the possibility that a smaller population might reduce growth — by reducing the opportunities for specialization, or by reducing the available pool of researchers.

But some people argue that a shrinking population is no problem — or might even be a good thing. When you make human workers scarce, it creates an incentive to invest in labor-saving technology, which boosts productivity. This mechanism has been proposed by some growth theorists, and some economic historians, like Robert Allen, even think this is what caused the Industrial Revolution! This effect might be strong enough to cancel out the aggregate effect of population aging, so that society stays just as rich — or even gets richer — due to low fertility rates.

This is actually a plausible mechanism. I have to say, I’m skeptical that it works in the general case. Human beings aren’t just labor supply; they also create labor demand. The incentive for businesses to buy new machine tools, robots, AI, etc. is that someone is going to buy the stuff they produce with those tools. If you have fewer people, you have fewer consumers. This is probably the reason why the effect of immigration on wages is typically close to zero. Babies are not that different from immigrants. A larger market size can also create an incentive for more rapid innovation — in fact, Acemoglu and Linn (2004) find that faster population growth increases pharmaceutical innovation.¹

But anyway, the idea that population scarcity stimulates innovation is the thesis of a new paper by Daron Acemoglu, David Autor, Keelan Beirne, and Andrew Scott. This is from the abstract:

Contrary to the widespread expectation that [low birth rates] hamper economic growth, we find lower birth rates are associated with higher growth in GDP per working-age adult across countries and higher wage growth across US commuting zones, with no negative impact on aggregate GDP or earnings. These patterns are not explained by educational upgrading, rising female labor force participation, the declining importance of agriculture, or neoclassical-Solow mechanisms. We argue that they reflect the endogenous, labor-saving response of technology to the scarcity of younger workers. Consistent with this interpretation, countries and regions with lower birth rates exhibit more labor-saving patents and growing high-tech activity. There is also higher TFP growth across countries and industries. [emphasis mine]

It’s a plausible result. But before we go on to the details of the paper, let’s talk about what this result would imply, if it does turn out to be true.

One of the paper’s basic theses is that technological automation raises wages. That flies in the face of the empirical work that Acemoglu has done on robots.² It also more broadly seems to contradict what Acemoglu has been saying about AI, both in his research papers and in his public statements. In his 2024 paper, “The Simple Macroeconomics of AI”, Acemoglu writes that “predicted TFP gains over the next 10 years [from AI] are…predicted to be less than 0.53%.” In his 2021 paper, “Harms of AI”, Acemoglu writes:

I argue that if AI continues to be deployed along its current trajectory and remains unregulated, it may produce various social, economic and political harms. These include: damaging competition, consumer privacy and consumer choice; excessively automating work, fueling inequality, inefficiently pushing down wages, and failing to improve worker productivity. [emphasis mine]

This stands in direct contradiction to Acemoglu’s new paper with Autor, Beirne, and Scott. If modern automation technologies push down wages without raising productivity, it cannot compensate for population aging in the way that Acemoglu, Autor, Beirne, and Scott claim that it must — and therefore, population aging is dangerous in a way that it wasn’t before.

Now, it’s fine for a researcher to find two seemingly contradictory things — or even put forward two contradictory theories — in two different papers. The real world is messy and complicated, and there are plenty of “puzzles” in the literature. But if Acemoglu goes around simultaneously telling us:

  1. not to worry about population aging, because automation will compensate for it with higher productivity and higher wages, and

  2. to worry a lot about automation, because it pushes down wages without raising productivity much…

…then we have a problem.³

But anyway, on to the actual details of Acemoglu et al. (2026). First of all, I’m not convinced by their result that lower birth rates raise per capita GDP at the country level. The reason is that once they control for a bunch of stuff — education, urbanization, geographic region, etc. — the result loses statistical significance. Here’s their Table 1, with the estimates I’m talking about circled in red:

In their abstract, the authors declare that “these patterns are not explained by educational upgrading, rising female labor force participation, the declining importance of agriculture, or neoclassical-Solow mechanisms.” But at least some of these patterns can apparently be explained by other things — initial education levels, urbanization, and so on — which makes the claim in the abstract a lot less impressive than it sounds.⁴

Also, note that the more controls the authors add, the weaker the estimated effect becomes. That’s generally a red flag in empirical papers. No matter how smart and careful you are, there are always things you don’t control for, especially in a cross-country regression, since countries differ in so many ways. So if the things you do control for tend to weaken your headline result by a lot, you should be worried that the rest of your result can be explained by the controls you left out.

For example, what about institutions, which Acemoglu has spent much of his career telling us are the main determinants of development? If the legacy of colonialism can be canceled out by passing out free condoms, why did Acemoglu win a Nobel prize? The word “institutions” does not even appear once in this new paper!⁵

A more realistic possibility is that lower birth rates in 1940 were correlated with other things — maybe a lot of other things — and that it’s these other things, rather than birth rates, that give rise to the correlation in the paper.

Of course, what we ultimately care about isn’t GDP per working-age adult⁶ — it’s GDP per capita. The authors have data on GDP per capita, but they barely mention it in the analysis;⁷ I’m not sure why. They do look at total GDP, and here they find no correlation, but a big standard error:

We shouldn’t interpret absence of evidence as evidence of absence. Cross-country regressions have small samples and tons of heterogeneity, so their standard errors tend to be huge — they just have trouble explaining much about the world. But the authors sort of blur this line, saying things like “no negative impact on aggregate GDP or earnings”, when really they should say “we can’t find a negative impact.” There could be a positive relationship between birth rates and growth hiding in that cloud of data points. (Sadly, this is standard practice in economics, but it makes a difference in how results get sold.)

Anyway, the result for wages in U.S. commuting zones holds up somewhat better. It’s a bit more statistically significant, and it doesn’t get attenuated as much by adding controls. But here, I’m worried about different issues: sorting and clustering. Basically, the result shows that coastal cities — places like New York City, San Francisco, Boston, etc. — had both lower birth rates in 1940 and faster wage growth from 1970 to 2020. The authors’ interpretation is that businesses in NYC, SF, and Boston had fewer workers, and so were forced to embrace labor-saving automation, while businesses in places like Birmingham, Alabama or Gary, Indiana refused to automate because they were endowed with plentiful cheap labor thanks to the legacy of an extra-large Baby Boom.

I am suspicious of this result, because American cities are not independent of each other. People can pretty easily move from Gary, Indiana to Boston, and vice versa! Ideas and capital can move even more easily — it’s pretty trivial for a company that patents a robot in Boston to actually put that robot to work in Gary. In fact, things like this happen all the time in America. Acemoglu and Restrepo (2017) note that the commuting zones with the greatest exposure to robots include Detroit, Lansing, Saginaw, Defiance, OH, Lorain, OH, Muncie, IN, Racine, WI, and Wilmington, DE.

Just to take one example of how different regions in America are dependent on each other, suppose that over the period from 1970 to 2020, Americans with lots of talent tended to move from Gary to Boston in order to take advantage of the increasing number of knowledge-industry jobs there. And suppose that at the same time, less talented Americans moved from Boston to Gary, in order to take advantage of the cheap land there. And suppose that high-value industries, like biotech and robotics and software, simultaneously decided to put their research labs in Boston rather than Gary because that’s where the best workers were headed.

In this case, you’d see Boston grow more than Gary, for reasons that had nothing to do with birth-rate-driven labor supply. Other research — for example, by Enrico Moretti — has shown that the sorting of talent and knowledge industries was strongly correlated with income divergences between American regions after 1970. Now, Acemoglu et al. do control for initial local education levels, but if sorting really began after 1970 (as Moretti has shown), that doesn’t really help. They also use “composition-adjusted” wages that try to model what local wages would be if education levels were held constant. But even if that adjustment is valid,⁸ it’s likely that a lot of skills aren’t captured by simply measuring who has a college degree.⁹

So in Acemoglu et al.’s telling, a substantial part of the reason the San Francisco Bay Area became Silicon Valley is not because the tech industry naturally tends to cluster in certain locations and draw in talented engineers and entrepreneurs, but because people in the Bay Area in 1940 didn’t have many kids, which forced Bay Area businesses to embrace automation instead. I simply don’t buy that story. I might eventually be persuaded to buy that story, but I don’t think this paper has sufficient evidence to persuade me yet.

Anyway, I am not claiming that Acemoglu et al. (2026) is a crappy paper. It’s clearly an important addition to the literature, and it deals with a very hard area of research where definitive results are very scarce. The basic idea is worth taking seriously. Maybe in a world where AI is growing by leaps and bounds, a scarcity of human workers should be the last thing on our minds!

But we shouldn’t regard this paper as definitive. And it contradicts a bunch of other research:

  • Kremer (1993) finds evidence that regions with faster population growth had faster technological progress.

  • The endogenous growth literature argues that because ideas are nonrival, larger populations are able to sustain faster technological progress — this is a basic assumption in Romer (1990), Jones (2022), and many other models.

  • Maestas, Mullen, and Powell (2023) find that aging was negatively correlated with productivity growth among U.S. states from 1980 to 2010;¹⁰ Ozimek, DeAntonio, and Zandi (2018) find something similar.

  • Aksoy et al. (2019) do a panel time-series regression across OECD countries from 1970 to 2014, and find that low fertility and low population growth are correlated with slower economic growth.

And even if Acemoglu et al. (2026) is right about the past, that doesn’t mean we can extrapolate it to the future. Jesús Fernández-Villaverde points out that you can’t necessarily do a linear extrapolation of effects at above-replacement fertility to effects at below-replacement fertility:

The fertility collapse now underway has no historical precedent. The seven decades of data the [Acemoglu et al. (2026)] paper analyzes, however carefully, contain nothing remotely comparable to the ultra-low fertility rates we observe today…

[T]he birth and fertility rates of 1950 provide little information about the consequences of the ultra-low birth and fertility rates we are experiencing today. Observations from a very different range of values are unlikely to capture the nonlinear cumulative effects of ultra-low birth and fertility rates…[E]ven in 1980, birth and fertility rates were not as low as they are today…A TFR of 1.56 means each generation is 76% the size of the last: the population declines about 0.9% per year, so after 100 years you retain roughly 40% of the initial population. A TFR of 0.75 means each generation is 37% of the last: about a 3.35% decline per year, leaving roughly 3.5% after a century. Hence, we are dealing with a factor of about 11. A TFR of 1.56 and a TFR of 0.75 both count as “low fertility” in a regression, but they are qualitatively different regimes. The 1980 variation the paper identifies lives in the gentle-decline world; nothing in their data resembles the second…

[W]e should not fool ourselves: we are sailing into demographic terra incognita, and in these waters, the pretense of knowledge is the most dangerous temptation.

In fact, Hayashi (2025) documents just such a nonlinear relationship between aging and growth, where countries with above-replacement fertility seem to benefit from lower birth rates, but countries with below-replacement fertility seem to do worse when their birth rates fall even further.¹¹

External validity and nonlinearity are big problems in much of growth economics, development economics, economic history, and so on (and often in other fields too). But it means that there’s a danger, when the world’s top economist writes a paper making big bold claims, that we end up deferring to that individual’s intellectual authority instead of recognizing the true uncertainty of the unprecedented changes our world is facing. I’m still very worried about the shrinkage of the human race, and I think you should probably still be worried too.

See also Acemoglu (2009), which theorizes that labor scarcity discourages the creation of technology that complements human labor:

The main result of the paper shows that labor scarcity will encourage technological advances if technology is strongly labor saving. In contrast, labor scarcity will discourage technological advances if technology is strongly labor complementary.

2

Acemoglu and Restrepo (2017) find that robots depress wages, whereas the entire mechanism in Acemoglu et al. (2026) relies on automation raising wages. Of course, Acemoglu might claim that robots are special, and not representative of automation technologies in general. But that would make the 2017 result a lot less important and generalizable than it was sold as being, back in 2017!

3

Also note that Acemoglu et al. (2026) can be read as an anti-immigration result. If young population growth stifles automation, doesn’t that mean we should restrict immigration in order to raise wages? That doesn’t mean the result is wrong, and it will certainly make MAGA types happy, but it does mean that it stands in conflict with the existing empirical literature on immigration and wages.

4

The “stacked differences” model does retain statistical significance after the inclusion of controls, but just barely. I wouldn’t put much faith in a borderline result like that.

5

The word “institutional” does appear once, but not as an explanatory variable for past patterns of growth:

At the same time, the demographic changes currently underway are accompanied by increased life expectancy (Scott, 2021, 2024), which may spur institutional changes, policies, and additional human capital investments that complement longer lifespans. These forces may counteract any negative effects of aging[.]

6

Actually, this is a bit beside the point, but I wish economists would stop using GDP per working-age adult as a measure of anything. Working-age adults are not some magical resource that creates GDP just by eating and breathing; they must actually work. Data on output per hour of work is readily available, and if it’s not available, output per employed person is usually a good proxy. I don’t see any good reason to use output per working-age adult. And you should NEVER mislabel output per working-age adult “output per worker”, as Acemoglu et al. (2026) do throughout their paper. Bad!!

Everyone hates the “elites,” but who are they?

According to voters, it’s basically just rich people.

Matthew Yglesias
Aug 20
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

Everyone likes to talk about “elites,” but what does that mean? Or what do people even think it means?

This week, Jerusalem and I discuss interesting polling from The Argument that asked Americans who they think the elites are. The answer is primarily the very rich, followed by celebrities and to a lesser extent business executives and elected officials.

The mass public largely rejects the conservative concept of an intellectual elite composed of professors, journalists, and people with advanced degrees and seems more aligned with the left-populist concept of anti-elitism as basically just hostility to rich people.

One point I raise is that the “celebrity” category may resolve some of the disjuncture here. After all, a famous and successful journalist or professor can shade into the celebrity category and therefore become elite. Certainly if what you’re interested in is social and political influence, then a famous journalist seems more elite than a similarly famous actor, athlete, or musician — while stipulating of course that the most famous actors, athletes, and musicians are much more famous than the most famous journalists.

My strongest disagreement with the voting public, though, is about its emphasis on the elite status of billionaires relative to business executives.

Of course, many billionaires are business executives and many business executives are billionaires. But to the extent that these categories become disjointed, I think someone like Walmart C.E.O. John Furner is a very important actor in American society even if his net worth is “only” in the low nine figures. To me, the whole point of a concept like “elite” is precisely to distinguish the idea of prestige and influence from mere wealth. Walmart founder Sam Walton’s grandson Lukas is a lot richer than the company’s present-day C.E.O. I’m happy to call him part of the elite just on the basis of his wealth, but, in practical terms, fewer people care what he thinks than pay attention to the views of Furner and other hired-gun C.E.O.s of major companies. Similarly, I would say that senators and four-star generals and admirals are absolutely part of the American elite despite receiving relatively modest compensation. What is the point of the term if not specifically to draw this distinction?

We also delve into some interesting findings about what most Americans believe the elite believes. Jerusalem notes that voters seem to perceive elites as disagreeing with them about basically everything. So most people believe in a government guarantee of health insurance and believe that elites do not support this. But most people oppose government ownership of most businesses, with a larger share saying that elites support the policy. Similarly, Americans believe that elites are against free trade and hold more traditional views about gender roles.

Jerusalem and I discuss all this and more, including the important question of whether we are elites.

Like, you really — it is very difficult to actually square this in a way that is going to produce good politics. And what it does produce, like, as you were saying, is a politics that is anti-growth, anti-housing, and even if in rhetoric is pro-immigrant, is hostile to immigrants.

Like, it is very, very difficult for immigrants to just, like, move into cities and societies where there is not cheap, readily available housing for them, for them to take advantage of. And it creates these horrible dynamics with existing low-income residents, as we saw in Chicago, when, instead of resolving kind of these bigger concerns, you know, you end up diverting fiscal resources to newcomers at the expense of, at the perceived expense of, old hats.

So I think there’s a level here which, I mean, both of us are small-L liberals here. You could be able to just embrace the light of liberalism and then we’ll all be good and we’ll have perfect pro-immigration politics forever.

Matthew Yglesias: Well, can I say? So here, we should close this out. But I thought the American people’s craziest take in this poll is that only 43% of people said that elected officials are elites.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And to me, in part to the point of what we’re just talking about here, right? It’s like elected officials are like paradigmatic elites. Like, the blue state governors who’ve been setting these carbon caps, these emissions targets, like, they are elite decision-makers. They are choosing to not reconcile the conflict between two —

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Like, competing moments of their commands. They are doing coalition management via incoherence and kicking the can down the road.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: They could choose differently. Journalists, I think, like ours at least, in a Hans Noel sense, the other thing that, like, you and I do, right, is we’re, like, doing these takes and we’re trying to say, like, guys…

Jerusalem Demsas: We’re coalition merchants.

Matthew Yglesias: …I understand that you have this log roll where the immigration lawyers and the environmental lawyers are, like, both have a seat at the table, but what they are saying is actually in conflict.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And, like, you need to think about this. And this is, this is what elites do, right? Because the mass public, God bless, is just, like, entitled to have these, somewhat superficial understandings of how these ideas fit together, and they’ll just affirm different things.

You know, like, immigrants, we get the job done. You know, climate is an existential threat. And it’s like elites need to construct a coherent policy agenda.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: That weighs these considerations. And the idea of a per capita versus an aggregate emissions target is, like, so fucking boring. Nobody halfway normal is going to care.

Like, it actually matters quite a lot. And this is why a responsible elite needs to handle these things better than we currently are.

Jerusalem Demsas: OK, well, let’s take a break, and when we come back, we’re going to do peer review.

All right, we’re back with peer review. Matt, what do you got for me?

Matthew Yglesias: We got a good one. This is — we’re delving into the truth of the American elite. We are looking at From Field to Firm: College Sports and Early-Stage Career Choice by Paul Gompers, George Hu, Will Levinson, and Sachin Srivastava. And so they are looking at hiring networks among Ivy League varsity athletes.

The headline finding here is that if you are employing one additional alumni from a specific Ivy League collegiate sports team — so you get a guy who played baseball at Yale — this increases the odds that another Yale baseball player will join your firm by 193.7%.

Jerusalem Demsas: Incredible effect.

Matthew Yglesias: We have grown accustomed in empirical social science to modest effect sizes being turned into a big deal, ‘cause people want to get their papers published.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: But this is a really big effect size. And then they showed they could tamp it down. So any Ivy League athlete who plays the same sport, right? So not just, like, another guy from Yale baseball, but from any Ivy League baseball team goes up 16.4%.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And then any athlete from the same university goes up 4.6%. So we can see people really like to hire their teammates. They also like to hire guys who they played against, and they have a modest inclination to just hire other sports bros who they went to school with.

Jerusalem Demsas: So one thing I’ll say is that the 193.7% is obviously a massive effect size. It sounds larger than I think it practically is because it’s a relative increase from a very small baseline probability. So I think it’s not implausible.

I think a couple interesting things that I started thinking about as a result of this paper. One is that the team connections dwarf the ordinary alumni connections or even the other guys who played sports, the same sport as you at a different school, or other guys who played sports at your school. And I think it indicates that the network of, the network benefits of being in these elite groups is, like, quite powerful.

And I would expect, like, they don’t actually show this in the paper obviously, but, like, I would expect, like, other things like eating clubs at Princeton or finals clubs at whatever school does that. I don’t remember which one. Is that the Harvard thing?

Matthew Yglesias: It is.

Jerusalem Demsas: Finals club. OK, finals clubs. You would know, Matthew. Finals clubs. Were you in finals club or no?

Matthew Yglesias: I was not in — it’s a final club, not a finals club. I was not in a final club, no.

Jerusalem Demsas: Wow. My apologies. The final clubs at Harvard.

Matthew Yglesias: I tried to get into the Signet Society, but I was blacklisted.

Jerusalem Demsas: Is that a secret society?

Matthew Yglesias: It’s an arts and culture organization. There is a prominent secret network of Signet Society alumni working…

Jerusalem Demsas: Is this just euphemistic?

Matthew Yglesias: …working in arts and media. No, I don’t know. I couldn’t get in.

Jerusalem Demsas: OK. Well, anyway, I would expect that other kind of small groups at elite colleges similarly play a really strong role, whether these kinds of things are fraternities or sororities or even debating societies, whatever it is. And, I mean, I will say this, one thing that people who are opposed to affirmative action will often say to me is that I am overrating how important access to these institutions actually is in order to achieve kind of broader goals of egalitarianism.

And this is not a dispositive study in my favor, but what I will say is that my perception as someone who did not attend a very elite university is that, actually, when I am now observing elites that I am around in D.C. all the time, they all seem to know each other from these specific clubs and things or from college they all went to together. And that clearly has had some sort of benefit to them.

And I will just say this: If you are someone who is discounting the importance of affirmative action here, one channel through which I think that it’s increasingly unlikely for you to be correct is that it just doesn’t matter whether you have more people of color going to these schools in order to shift what the composition of big firms or important companies looks like.

Matthew Yglesias: OK, so I guess two following points here. One that I think is a little bit in tension with your analysis is that, not different, but one reason that the effect is so large is that clearly actually knowing something carries a lot of value, right? And I think one thing about that is that it can lead people to actually overestimate the signaling value of having attended the school, right? So it’s like, the guy who played with you on your team is somebody who you know.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yes.

Matthew Yglesias: Right? These schools are fairly large. I went to college with a lot of people who I don’t know. And we sometimes now pretend that we knew each other, because we’re, like, working in politics in D.C. and are roughly the same age, but it’s like, it’s not true, you know.

Jerusalem Demsas: Oh, so everyone’s messing with me? They don’t actually know each other? Is that what you’re saying?

Matthew Yglesias: It’s to an extent, you know. I mean, it’s — no, I mean, you know, it’s like, you know, like, I know Rohit Chopra from American politics, and also he lived around the corner from me, and also we went to college at the same time, and we did, like, know some of the same people and stuff. And, you know, I don’t know, like, that’s a — but, like, I didn’t know him in school, you know, like, from back there. But we’re, like, part of some nebulous, like, Harvard mid-aughts blob.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: You know, along with other people. But it would be interesting to redo this with things that are not sports teams because your suppositions — like, if I had to pre-register my study, I think it would come out that way. But we don’t actually know. The other thing that I thought was — this is just whatever, but, you know, people used to talk about finance bros.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And then that verbiage, like, leapt to people started talking about tech bros. But one thing you could see here is that the athlete alone alumni network effect is way prominent in finance, very specifically in finance. And then it’s present but in an attenuated way in consulting, and it’s then present in a more attenuated way in law and in technology, but it’s quite attenuated when you get down there.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yes.

Matthew Yglesias: So there’s a real sense in which there are finance bros. Like, guys who played lacrosse in college are very prominent in the financial services industry. The tech industry, there’s a lot of men working in tech, but I don’t know that they’re bros.

Jerusalem Demsas: All men are bros. A brotherhood of equals.

Matthew Yglesias: That is not correct. And we see it here, right? It’s like —

Jerusalem Demsas: I was saying that in a beautiful egalitarian way. You are using it pejoratively. I think bros are good.

Matthew Yglesias: I love and respect the bros, but it’s, but it’s — bros are hiring bros.

Jerusalem Demsas: That’s true.

Matthew Yglesias: Like, that’s what we are seeing here. They are not just randomly hiring other Ivy League graduates. They’re hiring their own teammates. But it attenuates to people who weren’t their teammates, but they like other athletes, right? Because they themselves —

So whether it’s true or not that playing varsity collegiate sports demonstrates important things about character and leadership and discipline, you can understand that the people who played collegiate varsity sports think that that’s true.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: They’re like, “I was up at 5 a.m. rowing a fucking boat while these other losers were sleeping in or hungover or whatever.” And so they really respect and value that experience.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And, similarly, I mean, I think military veterans like to hire other veterans. Now, they like to hire people they knew, as do many people, but they respect the service as a credential in a way that other people might look at and be like, “Why the fuck were you getting up at 5 in the morning to row a boat? That’s stupid.”

Jerusalem Demsas: Matt, I respect our troops. What I will say is this.

Matthew Yglesias: I’m talking about crew athletes. We all respect the troops.

Jerusalem Demsas: OK. OK. I misunderstood. But I will say, I wish, I mean, this paper does a lot of stuff, so I’m not criticizing them, but I do wish I had more of a sense of the impact of these hiring decisions on firm quality or even self-reported anything from the firm. Because I don’t really know what my prior would be about whether these sorts of networks improve the productivity of these companies or whether it hampers them by reducing diversity of backgrounds so that you’re getting different kinds of people and not replicating the same person over and over again.

Seems interesting, seems difficult to know. It’s a pretty big sample size, like, what, 170,000 people that they’re following over 50 years? So maybe they can do some more slices of the data and run some analyses and see and maybe do some, I don’t know, some surveys, but seems hard because some of these firms were in the 1950s, so I don’t know how you would actually get that information.

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah, I mean, it’s also worth saying, I mean, they looked specifically at Ivy League colleges. Yeah. It might be interesting to see this more broadly.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah, sororities.

Matthew Yglesias: Well, no, so there’s, like, non-sports, but also just, like, you know, the sports, you know, there is a big athletics program at the University of Michigan.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And some of that is like D1 college football, which is like an eccentric and, like, a way bigger deal than Ivy League sports, but they also have lower sports. But it does also — people sometimes wonder about the recruiting of athletes for these obscure fancy sports. What’s the — I mean, colleges field basketball and football teams because those sports directly bring in fans and revenue.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: You never meet a college fencing super fan, but a lot of schools do have these programs. One reason for it is that a lot of alumni athletes just care a lot about these teams.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: They donate money and they pay it forward, and you can wonder why that is, but it’s like people feel these connections across space and time, and it manifests in their hiring. It’s like not — it might be good, it might be bad, it might be totally irrational, it might be actually, like, a great way to screen for employees, but it’s like, it’s not cheap talk.

Like, people are actually hiring other athletes, primarily not people who were high-end competitors in the most mainstream sports in America. These are mostly these kind of weird sports.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah. Well, I accidentally hired someone who did college debate, but I did not know this when I actually hired her. So I feel perhaps I’m perpetuating inequality by doing that.

Matthew Yglesias: You can tell a college debater from…

Jerusalem Demsas: I did not. She’s European.

Matthew Yglesias: …from like 20 feet away.

Jerusalem Demsas: That’s rude. She’s European. So it’s very, you know, who knows? All right. Well, this was great. Elites in all forms of this podcast. If you guys like this, please like, subscribe, tell your friends about the podcast, and we’ll see you next Thursday.

Matthew Yglesias: Bye.

The Case Against Bond Market Panic

Don’t let the Very Serious People undermine a progressive agenda — again

Paul Krugman
Aug 20
 
READ IN APP
 

Yesterday I wrote about how interest rates are rising around the world. I acknowledged that the higher rates are a real problem, but argued that there is no evidence that the U.S. faces a looming Greek-type debt crisis. Today I’ll talk about why it’s important for the future Democratic administration (assuming that we have free and fair elections in 2028) to keep a sense of perspective and not panic about the size of the federal debt.

Yes, as headlines in every newspaper are telling us, U.S. debt just hit $40 trillion —a number that is big and round, but otherwise has no special significance. More relevant is the incredible irresponsibility of the Trump administration, with its unfunded tax cuts that overwhelmingly benefit the wealthy, billions in wasteful military spending — redesigning aircraft carriers because Trump doesn’t like the way they look! — and more. Yet I don’t think that the U.S. faces a debt crisis. Specifically, I don’t think we will suffer a broad economic crisis brought on by investors’ loss of faith that the heavily indebted U.S. government will fail to pay what it owes.

I backed up that claim in yesterday’s post by citing market data showing that investors have little concern that the U.S. will default on its debt or that it will try to inflate the real value of the debt away. While such data are important, however, as some readers pointed out, they are not definitive because markets often fail to see even predictable crises coming. Some of us remember all too well the market’s complacency about housing in the 2000s, even though the signs of a massive bubble were everywhere one looked.

But anyone who asserts that markets are missing an impending debt crisis should be asked to explain how, exactly, such a crisis might play out. Don’t wave your hands at the debt crises that struck Greece and other southern European nations around 2010, because our situation is very different: Unlike Greece, which is a member of the euro area, the U.S. economy runs on dollars and U.S. government debt is denominated in dollars.

That matters because it’s very hard to construct a scenario for a Greek-style debt crisis in a nation that borrows in its own currency. As far as I can tell — and I’ve studied the issue at length — there are no historical examples in which this happened. The detailed, wonkish logic of why we are not and have never been Greece is explained in a paper I presented at the IMF’s annual research conference some years ago.

Yet the issue of whether a U.S. debt crisis was imminent was highly relevant at the time I presented that paper. Why? Because the Very Serious People were using scare stories about a potential debt crisis to demand fiscal austerity that delayed full recovery from the global financial crisis right to the end of the Obama administration, not to mention demanding cuts to Medicare and Social Security.

Who were the Very Serious People? Some were Republicans out to sabotage Obama. Others were self-important centrists. And the media played a big role. As Ezra Klein wrote in 2013,

For reasons I’ve never quite understood, the rules of reportorial neutrality don’t apply when it comes to the deficit. On this one issue, reporters are permitted to openly cheer a particular set of highly controversial policy solutions.

The VSPs, aka the debt scolds, went strangely silent once Trump took office the first time. Somehow massive revenue-losing tax cuts that further enriched the already wealthy didn’t alarm them as much as fiscal stimulus aimed at fighting mass unemployment.

But if Democrats control Congress and the White House in 2029, you can be sure that the Very Serious People will be back.

Paul Waldman had an excellent post on this recently, in which he made a prediction:

We know exactly what is going to happen once a Democrat is elected president — in fact, the ground will be seeded during the 2028 campaign. All of a sudden, the deficit will become an urgent matter that Democrats have to address, the subject of endless media coverage and fake concern from Republicans. Democratic plans for programs such as health care will be met once again with “But how are you going to pay for it?” Proposals for new commissions to recommend drastic budget cuts will be bandied about. Professional deficit scolds from organizations like the Peterson Institute will once again find themselves deluged with media requests. And because Democrats desperately want to be considered Serious People, they tend to react by saying “Oh yes, we take the deficit very seriously and we are committed to tackling it,” then find themselves hamstrung in their ability to govern.

Exactly. And the message for Democrats is clear: Don’t let the Very Serious People do what they did to Obama, using scaremongering about a debt crisis to block a progressive agenda.

I’m not saying that Democrats should be like Trump, and blithely ignore debt and deficits. They should by all means push for tax hikes on high incomes, close loopholes exploited by multinational corporations, strengthen IRS enforcement, and more. This could make a big difference: As Jared Bernstein and Bobby Kogan have shown, our deficit would be far more manageable if first Bush, then Trump, hadn’t rammed through tax cuts that hugely favored high-income Americans:

So Democrats should aim to restore the progressivity of the U.S. tax system, which would both help reverse our descent into oligarchy and help make the budget deficit more manageable. But the lesson from the Obama years is that they must not let themselves be intimidated by dire warnings about an imminent debt crisis. These warnings were totally wrong 15 years ago, and will still be wrong in 2029 even if interest rates remain relatively high.

In short, do not give in to debt panic.

Thousands of years of indoor air pollution

The too-late invention of somewhat safe ways to cook and heat with wood

Matthew Yglesias
Aug 20
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

I’ve been thinking lately about the question of historical realism in dramatic depictions of the past.

And also about chimneys.

Their absence isn’t always obvious in either fictional (such as “The Odyssey”) or fantastical (such as “House of the Dragon”) depictions of ancient life, but chimneys are a more recent invention than you might think.

Scientists today believe that humans have been making fires for at least 400,000 years. The chimney, by contrast, seems to have been invented in England sometime in the 12th century and only slowly gained popularity over the course of several centuries.

Very early humans were presumably making their fires outside. But to survive winter in even temperate climates, you need a heat source inside your shelter. And in the extreme cold of the Ice Age that afflicted the world 20,000 years ago, people most certainly needed shelter.

Archeologists believe that Ice Age humans spent much of their time in natural rock shelters enhanced by deliberate attempts at insulation and that they spent summer nights in dome structures. All of these would have been heated by fire, of course, but that just meant open hearths in the middle of the dome or cave — essentially a campfire, but inside.

And that was the basic state of home heat for many thousands of years.

People understood that you needed some kind of hole in the ceiling or everyone would suffocate and die. But the upshot is still that people were breathing absolutely filthy air all winter long — something you rarely see depicted on screen because it would be ugly and depressing.

And even though this is long gone as a mainstream concern in developed countries, indoor air pollution from open fires continues to be a major problem facing the global poor.

Cooking as a health hazard

Literally millions of people die every year due to respiratory and pulmonary problems caused by inhaling smoke indoors.

These numbers are thankfully falling, mostly due to economic development in Asia. But it’s nonetheless a huge problem.

You can see clearly that indoor air pollution deaths track the availability of electric, gas, or propane cooking facilities rather than reliance on coal, charcoal, wood, crop waste, or dung. Asia still has by far the most deaths but has also seen the biggest decline in recent years.

Recently there’s been a bit of an effort to foment panic about the indoor-air-quality impact of gas stoves versus electric in rich countries. But it’s obvious if you’ve ever seen a wood fire burning that the gap in particulate pollution — the stuff you see in visible smoke — between solid fuels and gas is enormous.

When you look at these stats, though, the good news is that the countries where people still don’t have access to cleaner fuel sources are mostly quite warm.

It’s horrifying to think of the millions of people dying prematurely every year in Africa and South Asia due to all the smoke they’re inhaling just from cooking. In 12th-century Europe you would have had the same cooking needs plus even more wood burned for overnight winter heat.

A chimney doesn’t provide perfect ventilation, as anyone who’s ever sat around a modern hearth can attest. But it’s an enormous step up from letting smoke accumulate around the ceiling and then leak out of a poorly insulated structure.

Wealth and waste

One aspect of this that I find fascinating is that even when chimneys did start to appear, they didn’t exactly take off like wildfire.

That’s partly because while a chimney makes your fire less likely to kill you, it also makes the hearth less effective at its core competency of warming the room. The whole point of the chimney, after all, is to funnel stuff away from you quickly and expel it outside the home. But that stuff is hot! Letting it diffuse through the air in the room means that a higher share of the stored energy in the firewood ends up heating your home. A standard fireplace set into the wall and ventilated by a chimney offers a good amount of radiant heat from the flames and the coals. But the convection heat — hot air and gases — is mostly just going up the chimney.

This convection heat is actually a majority of the total energy of the fire, so from the standpoint of a thrifty person trying to keep warm in conditions of fuel scarcity, the chimney seems like a bad deal.

The chimney upside that persuaded people, slowly but surely over a multi-century span of time, is that chimney use allows for a multi-floor building. The open hearth doesn’t really work in that setting, while a chimney can pipe smoke from a ground floor up out of the building through additional floors.

By the 16th century, English people were using coal rather than wood to heat their homes. And coal was really the killer app for chimneys. Coal made energy abundant enough that wasting heat was less of a problem. But coal requires better airflow than wood to burn, and in this respect chimneys are a big improvement on an open hearth. The hot air rushing up the chimney leaves behind a void that pulls in other air, ensuring a better-oxygenated fire.

In America, meanwhile, we had ample firewood, so in the 18th century Benjamin Franklin and David Rittenhouse started iterating on metal-stove designs that would do a better job than traditional fireplaces of channeling smoke out of the house while radiating heat into it.

Subscribed

In Germany, Scandinavia, and Eastern Europe, by contrast, innovation went in the direction of the masonry stove. There are a variety of national masonry-stove traditions, but the commonalities are twofold: the gases go through a convoluted path before reaching the flue to extract more heat before warm air leaves the house, and the structure is surrounded with a large thermal mass. The idea is that instead of the fire warming the air in the room, it warms the masonry structure itself and then the masonry sheds heat slowly throughout the night.

I went down a YouTube rabbit hole of people extolling the superior virtues of this design compared with the traditional American wood stove. And it is, indeed, much more efficient at translating wood energy into home heat.

The downside is that the mechanism itself is larger, more complicated, and harder to build. It’s also harder to keep clean. I think you should see the less efficient American metal-stove design not as an inferior technology but as a correct response to the Firewood Abundance enjoyed by Americans relative to Europeans — a transatlantic gap in energy efficiency that continues to this day.

Innovating late in the game

Another dimension of fire efficiency is how fully a given piece of wood combusts into gases rather than turning into ash or particulates. One of the reasons why a natural gas or propane stove is so much less polluting than a wood fire is that the combustion is much more complete. Wood is just not as good at this, but, even so, stove design makes a huge difference.

For example, I got a Solo Stove outdoor fire pit earlier this summer. They market these devices as creating “smokeless” fires, which sounds like total bullshit. And of course the fires you build in them are not genuinely smokeless.

But honestly, it comes a lot closer than I thought.

This is because, relative to a traditional campfire built on the ground, this stove creates a steadier flow of air by elevating the wood and having little holes in the bottom of the fire pit.

But the really clever bit is the hollow gap inside the walls of the fire pit and the second ring of holes at the top. This means that not only does the wood itself burn, but the smoke and soot that result from the combustion get hit with a second wave of hot air — creating a secondary burn and ensuring that relatively little smoke and particulate matter ultimately rises out of the pit.

They, of course, sternly warn you not to use your fire pit inside and I, of course, have not. But obviously if you took this technology back in time several hundred years to the period when everyone was heating their homes with chimney-less fires, it would be a huge improvement.

In a sense, then, this is an example of a product category that is the opposite of “ahead of its time.” The first smokeless pits came on the market around 2011 rather than 1,000 years ago when they would have been more broadly useful.

By the same token, the best way to use biomass fuel for cooking is a “rocket stove,” which is based around a relatively narrow tube in the shape of an L or a J. The long, narrow, vertical tube (in effect a chimney) concentrates the heat from the fire and creates a powerful draft. The short horizontal tube pulls in a very concentrated blast of fresh air. This ensures highly complete combustion of the fuel and maximizes the amount of heat energy that goes into the pot or pan on top of the stove. It’s both more economical and cleaner than conventional biomass cooking.

This, again, would have been useful essentially throughout all of human history, but it was invented in Oregon in the 1980s by a team looking to address indoor air pollution in poor countries.

It’s a great design, but by the time of its invention, even a cleaner biomass stove was still really dirty compared with electricity or propane.

But for the vast majority of human history, everybody everywhere was relying on biomass cooking and would have benefited from these innovations. Permaculture weirdos have even perfected the rocket mass heater, which combines principles from the rocket stove and the masonry stove to create the ultimate high-efficiency wood-burning stove — that’s cool, but you can just heat your home with gas or electricity, which are better.

Serious problems with minimal attention

I suppose I should link this back to a timely political controversy, perhaps argue that the history of the chimney goes to show that Abdul El-Sayed should reflect on why he’s doing worse than every other frontline Dem Senate nominee and find some ways to move to the center.

But that doesn’t really make much sense.

In some European cities, especially in Denmark, they rely heavily on “district heating” where instead of having pipelines ship gas to individual home furnaces, the heat itself is piped to homes. If we had that kind of infrastructure, we could capture waste heat from data centers and pipe it into the district heating system to improve the overall efficiency of our energy infrastructure.

Unfortunately, not only is constructing this kind of infrastructure in the United States unlikely, but in practice people probably want to keep data centers far away from houses, which would make repurposing the waste heat less appealing.

I guess the winning linkage is that while the closure of the Strait of Hormuz is annoying Americans via higher gasoline prices, a much more substantively serious problem is that it has induced shortages of liquefied petroleum gas in middle-income countries.

That means lots of people have switched back to biomass cooking at least part time with predictably dire consequences for their respiratory health.

Subscribed

This returns us to where we started, which is that indoor-air-quality issues are well known and well understood in the sense that experts do not dispute their existence, but they’re also highly neglected. The modern attention economy creates incentives to pay attention to things other people are already fighting about and to ignore long-simmering problems — even when they’re directly adjacent to big newsworthy events.

But if you actually care about improving things, it’s important to find time to talk about stuff that isn’t the same thing everyone is already screaming about.

Scott Bessent Fails to Gaslight the Market

What doth it profit a man if he sell his soul and can’t even manipulate the 30-year?

Paul Krugman
Aug 21
 
READ IN APP
 

Scott Bessent, the Treasury Secretary, isn’t the worst member of Trump’s cabinet. I mean, he has to compete with the likes of Pete Hegseth. But he leads the pack in terms of being far worse than anyone imagined he would be. Here, for example, is how the Financial Times reported on his selection:

Credible Treasury secretary, my, um, assets. In office, Bessent has been a consummate Trump sycophant. For example, in March 2026 the Treasury announced that henceforth Donald Trump’s signature would appear on paper currency — a first for any sitting president. Bessent’s prepared remarks ran as follows:

Under President Trump’s leadership, we are on a path toward unprecedented economic growth, lasting dollar dominance, and fiscal strength and stability. There is no more powerful way to recognize the historic achievements of our great country and President Donald J. Trump than U.S dollar bills bearing his name, and it is only appropriate that this historic currency be issued at the Semiquincentennial.

This kind of “Dear Leader” rhetoric coming from the nation’s top economic official is far worse than just embarrassing. In times of crisis, the Treasury secretary’s credibility is a critical asset for dealing with financial markets. So when Bessent talks like a love-struck Natalie Harp, it carries the potential for enormous financial and economic costs for the country.

Moreover, Bessent routinely makes assertions about the state of the economy that are manifestly, glaringly untrue – as if he can gaslight the professionals who closely track economic data. A couple of weeks ago, for example, Bessent rejected the widespread view that we have a “K-shaped economy” in which a few people are doing well but many are falling behind:

I get sick of hearing about this K-shaped economy, I can say here definitively, the K-shaped economy is over.

Bessent tried to back up his claim by pointing to data on wages, which showed that those in the top 25 percent had slightly lower wage gains than those in the bottom 25%. But nobody familiar with the data was fooled. High-income Americans receive much of their income from capital, not labor, while many lower-income Americans rely on food stamps and other programs that are facing savage cuts under Trump. Here’s what after tax-and-transfer real income looks like for the 1 percent and the bottom half of the population since Trump II began:

Looks pretty damn K-ish to me.

So it’s clear that Bessent’s pronouncements are geared to an audience of one: Donald Trump. He doesn’t mind sounding like a fool and a liar to the financial markets and to the American public as long as it pleases Dear Leader.

But Bessent’s betrayal of the trust that was placed in him by the American public to be a competent steward of the nation’s economy goes beyond public pronouncements. Something very troubling is happening inside the Treasury department as well. According to the Partnership for Public Service, a nonpartisan watchdog, 7 out 16 Trump Treasury appointees confirmed by the Senate — that is, the very top Treasury officials — have left since the start of Trump II. That’s 44 percent, an astonishingly high percentage. According to NOTUS, which reported on the study,

At least four of the seven top Treasury officials left after disagreements with the White House over demands to stretch, if not violate, tax law. Those disputes included Treasury resistance to a controversial push to use taxpayer data as part of the administration’s immigration crackdown, as well as the president’s push to establish a $1.8 billion fund to compensate allies as part of a deal with the IRS to drop any past or future tax audits of the president and his family. (The “anti-weaponization” fund was later dropped due to resistance from Senate Republicans.)

NOTUS quotes Mark Mazur, a former senior Treasury official, who suggests that some of the departing officials may be leaving rather than commit illegal acts:

A lot of these people expect to have a career after this administration, and being disbarred would be a bad thing for them.

And aside from apparently demanding that Treasury officials act in ways that would put them in legal jeopardy, Bessent has been deploying the financial resources of the Treasury in ways that have little relationship to U.S. national interest, but are clearly in the service of Trump’s political goals.

One example was a large financial intervention in October 2025 to support the Argentine peso. The U.S. has no obvious economic or national security stake in Argentina. The obvious goal, however, was an attempt to rescue the right-wing, Trump-friendly government of Javier Milei. While this intervention bought Milei some time, it didn’t revive his political fortunes: Milei’s approval ratings are at Trump-like levels.

Which brings me to Bessent’s most recent interventionist move: An attempt to reverse the recent spike in U.S. long-term interest rates by buying back 30-year Treasury bonds. It’s actually an almost pitifully small move:

Still, where does the money for the buyback come from? From sales of government issued shorter-term debt, largely Treasury bills.

This is just a swap of longer-term government debt for shorter-term, riskier government debt. It does nothing to resolve the underlying U.S. fiscal problems that caused the spike in the 30-year debt. Some analysts call Bessent’s strategy“rearranging the deck chairs on the Titanic.”

But it’s actually worse than that. I won’t go into all the wonky details here, but Bessent’s bond move is functionally equivalent to “quantitative easing,” the policy the Federal Reserve followed in the early 2010s.

Back then the Fed was trying to boost an economy that was still deeply depressed in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis. So it tried to reduce long-term interest rates by buying long-term federal debt, paid for by effectively issuing short-term debt in the form of interest-paying deposits.

The Fed did quantitative easing in the early 2010s for good reasons: to resuscitate a moribund economy. But conditions are completely different now: Unemployment is fairly low and the economy is suffering from above-target inflation. Indeed, there’s a live debate within the Fed about whether to tighten money to fight inflation. So why is the Treasury engaging in an end run around the Fed, conducting its own de facto expansionary monetary policy?

The answer is clearly political: High long-term interest rates are an embarrassment for the Trump administration, and Bessent is trying to make the picture look prettier, even though this means undermining the people who are supposed to be making monetary policy.

The maneuver is failing: 30-year yields fell briefly on Wednesday, when the policy was announced, but bounced back on Thursday and were higher as I write this than they were a week ago. — clear proof that you can’t gaslight the bond market.

So Bessent, a former bond trader himself, has squandered all of his credibility with his sycophancy, his apparent demands that top officials engage in unethical and probably illegal conduct, and his abuse of the Treasury’s financial power for clearly political goals.

And his ruined reputation will be a real problem if and when, like many of his predecessors, he encounters a crisis in which we really need a credible Treasury secretary with competent subordinates.
